chapters.summary: Council staff welcomes attendees to the joint Fire and Emergency Management/Hospitals hearing, asks that electronics be silenced, and instructs anyone wishing to testify to see the sergeants at arms. Staff tells the public not to approach the dais and invites the chair to begin.
chapters.title: Council staff opens hearing and gives housekeeping instructions

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Welcome to the Committee on Fire Emergency Management, Joint Web Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, we ask that you please silence all electronics.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: If you wish to testify, please see one of the sergeant arms in the back.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: And at no point, please do not approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

chapters.summary: Chair Joann Ariola calls the joint oversight hearing to order, acknowledges members present and co-chair Mercedes Narcisse, and states the committees will examine ambulance response times and Intro 990. She explains the bill would use Notify NYC to alert residents to extended ambulance wait times.
chapters.title: Ariola opens hearing on ambulance response times and Intro 990

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: My name is Joanne Areola and I am chair to the Fire and Emergency Management Committee.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would like to begin by acknowledging council members who are here today, Council Members Shulman and Palladino.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I would also like to thank Chair Mercedes Narcisse for co-chairing today's hearing with me.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Today, the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management, along with the Committee on Hospitals, will once again be holding an essential oversight hearing on ambulance response times

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and discussing Intro 990, a bill I introduced that would require NYC to alert New Yorkers through the Notify NYC system of extended wait times for an ambulance.

chapters.summary: Ariola says that over the summer 700 calls were held in the EMS system due to staffing shortages. She argues Intro 990 would let New Yorkers know when help is not moments away and requires emergency notifications when FDNY EMS has more than 25 pending ambulance dispatches.
chapters.title: Ariola cites 700 held EMS calls and introduces 'minutes matter' alert bill

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Over the summer, we saw 700 calls being held by EMS system because of a lack of staffing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This minutes matter bill would let New Yorkers know what that system is

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: in the state of emergency and if you're called to 911 at the time, help is not moments away.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The Fire Committee will also hear Introduction 990 sponsored by myself, which requires the city to issue emergency notifications each time the FDNY EMS has more than 25 pending ambulance dispatches at any given time.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks EMTs, paramedics, and firefighters for delivering critical emergency medical care and responding to more than 1.6 million medical calls annually. She says EMS workers face stressful conditions, long hours, and are vastly underpaid despite their life-saving work.
chapters.title: Ariola honors EMS and first responders, notes 1.6 million medical calls

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As we all know, our first responders, notably our EMTs and paramedics, but also firefighters, are tasked with delivering critical emergency medical care throughout our city.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: These dedicated public servants routinely provide life-saving care and respond to more than 1.6 million medical calls each year.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We are forever grateful for your service.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: At this time, we must acknowledge that the EMS workers undertake an immensely difficult job due to stressful work conditions, long hours, and challenging work.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Not only that, EMS workers, particularly employed by the FDNY, are vastly underpaid.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For the vital jobs that they do.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yet despite these obstacles, each day thousands of ambulance workers strive tirelessly to serve the city and deliver timely emergency medical care to all New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Ariola says the city has struggled to provide timely emergency medical care despite publishing response-time data and reallocating resources. She notes FDNY response times have consistently increased over the past decade, especially for life-threatening incidents.
chapters.title: Ariola says response times to life-threatening emergencies have worsened

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Despite a dedicated and talented workforce, it is apparent

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: to anyone paying attention that our city has struggled to meet its obligations to provide timely emergency medical care to all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Each year, the city publishes substantial amounts of data related to emergency response times, a key metric to monitor when seeking to evaluate, improve the delivery of pre-hospital emergency care.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: In fact, according to the FDMY, the department regularly reviews response times to life-threatening medical emergencies across the city and develops strategies and reallocates resources to reduce response times

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: in communities with higher response times.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: However, over the past decade, FDNY's response times to emergency medical incidences have consistently increased, a trend that is seen dramatically in responses to life-threatening medical incidences.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The dire medical emergencies where prompt delivery of emergency medical service

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and care is most vital.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'm extremely concerned that New Yorkers are facing negative health outcomes due to the delays of the delivery of emergency medical care

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and the worry this instills a lack of public confidence in our city's ability to provide vital services when they are most needed.

chapters.summary: Ariola says she expects FDNY testimony to explain rising response times and cover dispatching, staffing, and ambulance maintenance. She also calls for broader discussion of pre-hospital emergency resources, interagency coordination, and reversing the trend before thanking staff and yielding to Narcisse.
chapters.title: Ariola outlines expectations for FDNY testimony and thanks committee staff

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As chair of fire and emergency management committee, I expect to hear testimony from the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: that will provide clarity to why we have seen dramatic increases in response times to medical emergencies and learn more about the department's procedures related to dispatching, staffing, and the maintenance of ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But also, I hope the department and administration is able to speak more broadly of the commitment of dedicating increased resources to the provision of pre-hospital emergency and truly examine agency operations

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and interagency coordination.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: To identify how the city can reverse this troubling trend of increasing emergency response times.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Because we cannot continue down this path, I'd like to thank our committee staff, our committee counsel, Josh Kingsley, our legal analyst, Will Hongash, and my amazing chief of staff, Phyllis Incerillo.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I will now yield to Chair Narcisse for her opening remarks.

chapters.summary: Chair Mercedes Narcisse apologizes for her delay and introduces herself as chair of the Committee on Hospitals and a registered nurse. She says delayed ambulance response and prolonged emergency department waits are urgent challenges facing New York City.
chapters.title: Narcisse opens Hospitals Committee remarks on ambulance delays

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Good morning and thank you for being here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I have to apologize for my five minutes or seven minutes delay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It should not happen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Good morning again to all of you and for being here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I am Chair Mercedes Narcisse, Committee on Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Actually from different aspects of my life being a registered nurse, and I'm so happy that we're having this hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Delayed ambulance response and prolonged emergency department wait times have become an increasingly urgent challenge in New York City.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says New York City has 49 hospital emergency departments, including 11 operated by NYC Health + Hospitals, serving more than 8.5 million people. She reports that from 2022 to 2025 H&H patients waited an average of 12.8 hours to transfer from the emergency department to an inpatient bed.
chapters.title: Narcisse cites H&H emergency department waits and overcrowding

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: While many factors contribute to these delays, one of the most significant is the growing strain on our health care system.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: New York City is home to 49 hospital emergency departments, including 11 hospitals operated by NYC Health and Hospital, HNH.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's where I used to work, which served more than 8.5 million New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Reports indicate that between 2022 and 2025, patients at H&H hospitals waited an average of 12.8 hours to be transferred from the emergency department to an inpatient bed.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: This prolonged wait can delay critical treatment, disrupt continuity of care, and contribute

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: to overcrowded emergency rooms.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As a registered nurse who work in triage at Elmer's Hospital Emergency Department, I have witnessed these challenges firsthand.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Before first responders can return to the field and answer the next emergency call, patients must be registered, assessed, and safely transferred into the care of hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: When emergency departments are overcrowded and inpatient beds are not available on the floor, that process can take far longer

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: than it should, creating a ripple effect throughout the entire emergency response system.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says staffing shortages, hospital closures, and barriers to primary care caused by federal Medicaid cuts have intensified pressure on the emergency system. She warns that temporary fixes will not help New York City.
chapters.title: Narcisse blames staffing shortages, closures, and Medicaid cuts for strain

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Staffing shortage.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Shortages, hospital closures, and increased barriers to accessing primary and preventive care due to recent federal Medicaid cuts we call HR1.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: One big, not beautiful, you know where I'm going.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Have further intensified these pressures.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says she is committed to finding long-term solutions rather than temporary fixes and recounts a family forced to drive their child to the hospital after a long ambulance wait. She says every resident deserves timely emergency care regardless of zip code, income, race, gender, immigration status, or background.
chapters.title: Narcisse calls for long-term solutions and cites child driven to hospital

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: As chair of the Committee on Hospitals, I am committed to examining the many factors driving prolonged ambulance response times and identifying

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: meaningful long-term solutions rather than temporary fix.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Temporary fix is not going to help us in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: New Yorkers deserve confidence that when they call for help during a medical emergency, and we know what took place recently.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They were waiting for so many minutes that the family forced to drive their own child to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That should not happen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Assistance will arrive as emergency assistance will arrive as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Every resident, regardless of zip code, income, race, gender, immigration status or background, deserves timely access to emergency care.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says the committees look forward to hearing from FDNY, emergency management, and other representatives about changes since the 2024 hearing and feedback on pending legislation. She thanks committee staff, says the city must lead by example, and calls health care a human right.
chapters.title: Narcisse previews FDNY/H&H testimony and backs health care as a human right

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Today, we look forward to hearing from New York City Fire Department, New York City,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: emergency management and other representatives in the field of emergency management about the alarming state of ambulance response times across the city,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: including what changes have been made since the last city council hearing on this topic in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And other city-supported efforts.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We also seek their feedback on the legislation before the committee today.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Together, we must work to ensure that our city ambulance services are efficient and trustworthy and that they continue to serve our residents with the best possible care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Like I always said, we call ourselves the capital of the world.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have to lead by example.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And health care is a human right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Without your health, you're nothing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we each, everyone in this room, can agree to that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Without your health, you're nothing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we have that responsibility to address that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Before we begin, I'd like to thank committee staff, senior legislative counsel, Ria Agosarara, legislative analyst, Raina Lee, policy analyst, Minna Butt,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: financial analyst Molly Howard and assistant director Florentine Cabarro for their hard work in preparing on this hearing and I also like to thank my staff for their hard work

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And as we continue to serve our constituents and the city as large.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we're all responsible to make sure this city is the best city.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I'll pass it on to my colleague, Chair Ayola.

chapters.summary: Ariola says the committees will give a courtesy to Jennifer Daly before swearing in the panel. She explains Daly is the mother of Kevin, a 14-year-old who had a medical episode at school and whose nurse called 911 three times without an ambulance arriving.
chapters.title: Ariola introduces Jennifer Daly as first courtesy witness

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Before we swear in the panel, we are going to give a courtesy to Jennifer Daly.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: She's going to testify first this morning.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Jennifer is the mother of Kevin, a 14-year-old boy who experienced a medical episode when he arrived at school on a late September morning.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The school nurse called 911 three times, but the ambulance never arrived.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Daly is joining us via Zoom to tell her story.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Daly, can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Yes, hi, how are you?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Oh, thank you for having me.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Jennifer Daly testifies remotely that her son Kevin arrived at St. Francis Prep feeling faint and weak, and the school nurse called 911 as his symptoms worsened. She says after multiple 911 calls and no ambulance, her husband advised their daughter to give Kevin aspirin, and she drove him to New York Presbyterian in Queens where he was diagnosed with a stroke.
chapters.title: Jennifer Daly describes son Kevin's stroke and ambulance no-show

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So, well, first I'd like to say thank you for having this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: It means a lot to me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So on September 28th, my son arrived at school around 8.15, and he was feeling fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: He arrived at school, and once he went into the building, he said he was feeling a little faint, a little weak, and his eye was blurry a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So he immediately went over right to the nurse's office, and he told her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: She sat him down, and she gave him water, and she gave me a phone call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: That phone call was about 8.17, and I instantly said, I'll be right there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So I left Howard Beach and drove over to St.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Francis Prep in Fresh Meadows.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And unfortunately, it was taking me a little longer than it normally does due to the morning commute traffic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And in the interim of getting there, I had received another phone call from her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And she stated to me that she thinks that she needs to call the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So I said, please do whatever you have to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: If the ambulance gets there before I do, you know, just tell me where you are.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: I will meet you there right away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And then I...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Was driving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the traffic was building up a little bit longer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And the nurse had called me again and said that she called the ambulance and she had

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: two sisters down there in the nurse's office with him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And his face looked, you know, a little, a little strange.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Like his eye was like, you know, not drooping, but his eye was slanting down a little bit and looked a little weird.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So she was going to make another phone call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So she made another phone call to the 911.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: My daughters went there and one of my daughters, they're both, actually one of my daughters is taking health and safety class, CPR training, first aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And she looked at her brother and said, he looks like he's having a stroke because they are learning that in school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: She immediately called my husband, who is a retired fireman as well, and he was at work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And she told him Kevin's symptoms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And my husband said, well, give him aspirin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Luckily, I'm an erotic and my kids have, you know, aspirin and Tylenol and Motrin on them in case they need it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And she gave him the aspirin right there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: In the midst of that phone call with my daughter, with my husband, I get another phone call from the nurse that she called the ambulance twice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And that he does need to go.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So I said, okay, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: I will be there any second.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: So when I arrived, he was there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: I saw him and he definitely 100% was having signs of a stroke.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: You can tell it like, or almost immediately.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: He was slurring his words.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: His speech wasn't clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: He didn't really know what he was speaking about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: He was mumbling his words.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And I'm

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: I called his cardiologist and I said, we have to get him over to, you know, the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: What do I do?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: She said, wait for the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: I said, I cannot wait for the ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: This is the going to be the third time that prep made the phone call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And my husband made a phone call to them as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And she said, okay, take him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: She called over to New York Presbyterian in Queens, and I rushed him over there with my twins from St.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Francis Prep.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: I think I got left prep at like 9.30 something, 9.32, and I got to Presbyterian at...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: 9.52, and my husband arrived as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: When we got there, he ran him in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: They were great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: They took him right away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: They gave him all kinds of tests, EKG, ultrasound, CAT scan, MRI, and he had a stroke.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Then they transferred him over to the hospital, Morgan Stanley Children's Hospital on 165th Street in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: And then he stayed there for several days until he was released.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: That's basically it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: That's my story.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Daly for sharing her story and says her daughters' preparation and her husband's medical knowledge likely saved Kevin's life. She reassures Daly that she was not neurotic but a great mother.
chapters.title: Ariola thanks Jennifer Daly and commends her family's quick action

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Daly, thank you for sharing your story.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And we're so thankful that you had the presence of mind to have your daughters prepared in case they did have any type of, you're not neurotic, you're just a great mom.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And the fact that your husband had the medical knowledge to tell your daughter to administer the aspirin because it could be probably life-saving.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Oh, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: I appreciate it from the bottom of my heart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We have one.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Chair Narcisse, you have to say something.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: No, no, don't go anywhere.

chapters.summary: Narcisse thanks Daly for saving her child's life and acknowledges her husband's FDNY background. She explains the school nurse could not administer medication without a doctor present, making the family's intervention especially critical.
chapters.title: Narcisse thanks Daly and explains school nurse medication limits

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want to say thank you to you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Oh, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For actually saving your child's life.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You did it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And, and.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm thankful for your husband, FDNY, as well.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I have to let you know that the nurse could not give that medication because without a doctor present.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So that's the reason the call you made to have the medication, be able to call on your daughter, your family to do that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's very much appreciated by us because you can save the life.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And unfortunately, the nurse would not give the medication.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jennifer Daly
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola notes that Council Members Maloney, Wong, and Brooks-Powers have joined and introduces the panel: Dr. Josh Motzquist from Health + Hospitals and FDNY Chiefs John Esposito, Paul Miano, and Denise Werner. Council staff administers the oath to affirm truthful testimony.
chapters.title: Ariola notes additional members and swears in FDNY/H&H panel

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yep, I would like to just note that we've been joined by council members, Virginia,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Maloney, my gosh, Councilmember Wong and Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, we will now swear in our panel consists of Dr.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Josh Motzquist from Health and Hospital, Chief Paul Maiano from the FDNY, Chief John Esposito from the FDNY,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and Chief Denise Werner from the FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for joining us today.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Hey, everyone.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Can you just raise your right hand and just affirm the following, that you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and answer honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Seeing you affirm, you may go ahead and testify.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chief, you may begin.

chapters.summary: FDNY Chief of Department John Esposito testifies that response times are increasing and unacceptable, and says addressing them is a top priority for him, the fire commissioner, and the mayor. He cites declining ambulance in-service hours and rising life-threatening call volume, saying FDNY is responding to more calls with fewer ambulances.
chapters.title: Esposito says EMS response times are a top FDNY priority

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Areola and members of the Fire and Emergency Management Committee, and Chair Narcisi and the members of the Hospitals Committee.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: My name is John Esposito, and I am the Chief of Department of the New York City Fire Department.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I am joined today by Paul Miano, Chief of EMS, and Denise Werner, Chief of EMS Dispatch.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: For members of FDNY EMS, reaching a patient experiencing an emergency quickly is paramount.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: When lives are at stake, every second counts.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As we have testified to this committee previously, the department is currently engaged in a challenging period of increasing response times.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We know this is unacceptable, and we are working tirelessly to reverse this trend.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I am grateful for the opportunity today to discuss some of the reasons for these increases and the steps that we are taking to fix it.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I want to state unequivocally that addressing EMS response times is a top priority for myself, the fire commissioner, and for the mayor.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: There are numerous reasons we are seeing increases in response time.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: One major factor is the number of in-service hours of ambulances in the 9-11 system.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As you can see from the most recent Mayor's Management Report, the average ambulance

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: in-service hours per day has trended lower over the most recent five-year period, from 8,891 in fiscal year 22 to 8,572 in fiscal year 25

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: and 8,109 in fiscal year 26.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the number of life-threatening medical calls has increased now compared to five years ago, from 564,412 calls in fiscal year 22

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: to a total of 610,771 calls in fiscal year 26.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Put another way, when comparing these snapshots, we are responding to more calls with fewer ambulances.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: After years of seeing increases in call volume every year, the total number of calls was slightly down over the last year.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: However, it remains a very high total number of calls.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Many of which are low-acuity calls that may be more appropriately served by non-emergency medical services.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: If a person is not experiencing an emergency, an ambulance is not always the appropriate means of transport.

chapters.summary: Esposito says decreased ambulance hours are significantly driven by staffing changes, including 358 EMTs and 63 paramedics who left EMS to become firefighters in 2026. He says the department staffs up before promotions but the effect on EMS staffing remains severe.
chapters.title: Esposito details EMS staffing losses to firefighter promotion cycle

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: A significant reason for the number of ambulance in-service hours that the number of in-service hours have decreased is staffing changes.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We are in the midst of a promotion cycle in

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: which 358 emergency medical technicians and 63 paramedics departed EMS to become firefighters in 2026.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: In 2025, 288 EMTs and 48 paramedics made this transition.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It's a positive outcome for the city to have firefighters with EMS and paramedic-level medical training, but it also has a severe impact on EMS staffing in the short term.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: When a class of EMS members enters the fire academy, it means that EMS leadership has hundreds fewer members to staff ambulances.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have taken measures to mitigate this impact, including deliberately staffing up above headcount prior to the promotion cycle.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But with so many members taking the firefighting exam in each cycle, the effect on EMS staffing continues to be significant.

chapters.summary: Esposito says 19 hospitals have closed since 2003, forcing ambulances to travel farther and reducing hospital-run ambulance contributions to the 911 system. He notes the system is about two-thirds municipal FDNY units and one-third hospital-run units, and says any lost tours add stress.
chapters.title: Esposito ties response times to hospital closures and lost voluntary units

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: There are also elements that influence response times that are unrelated to staffing.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Since 2003, 19 hospitals in New York City have closed, with the most recent closure in 2025.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That means fewer destinations for patients.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: With each closure, ambulances must travel further to get the patient to the emergency room and further again to travel back to their assigned area.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Hospital closures also mean fewer hospitals contributing ambulances to respond in the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Currently, the 911 system is made up approximately two-third municipal units operated by FDNY members and one-third hospital-run units that are staffed by the hospitals.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've also experienced hospitals reducing the number of units that they contribute to the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Each of those lost tours adds stress on the system.

chapters.summary: Esposito says FDNY must replace members who left EMS for firefighter positions or due to wages and schedules, and recruitment has become harder since COVID-19. He says the EMT union is negotiating with the city and hopes a contract resolution will boost recruiting.
chapters.title: Esposito says recruitment and contract talks are key to rebuilding EMS

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We are pursuing numerous adjustments and innovations to address the ongoing challenges with response times.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We know that building up EMS staffing is a key part of this issue.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We need to replace the members who have left EMS to become firefighters and other EMS members who have left.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Due to issues with wages, schedules, or for their own reasons.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Recruiting has become more difficult since the COVID-19 pandemic.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The union that represents the department's EMTs is currently at the negotiating table with the city's Office of Labor Relations, and we are hopeful that a resolution to the next contract will provide a recruiting boost.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Restoring staffing is a large piece of the puzzle, but it is not the only way we are attacking this problem.

chapters.summary: Esposito describes steps already taken, including paramedic response units, a centralized resource coordination center, and a borough-based command structure. He says these changes aim to get more ambulances into service and allow chiefs to tailor responses to local conditions.
chapters.title: Esposito lists operational changes: PRUs, CRCC, borough commands

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We are also working internally with external partners to re-examine existing practices, streamline processes,

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: and eliminate inefficiencies.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've already taken several steps to improve responses.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Paramedic response units.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've set up PRUs to get additional paramedics into the field who can respond to patients faster to assess, provide treatment, and arrange transport.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The paramedic response unit brings paramedics to assignments classified as life-threatening.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: However, if the assessment reveals that the patient does not require advanced life support, they are transferred to a basic life support unit, and the paramedics become available for the next high acuity assignment.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We currently have 14 of these units operating across the city.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The CRCC, we've created a centralized unit that assesses personnel across all divisions in real time with the aim of pairing up available members to get more ambulances into the field.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Our goal is to get as many units onto the street whenever possible to respond to calls and take the burden off of all the other units in the system.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The Borough-Based Command Structure.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Under this administration, EMS leadership has moved to a borough-based command structure.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This enables staff chiefs to provide more oversight over smaller areas so they can react quicker and more dynamically to evolving conditions in the field.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: These chiefs develop better localized knowledge and are able to provide tailor-made solutions to operational issues rather than a one-size-fits-all solution that may not be appropriate for a given geographical area.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The Borough Resource Coordination Center.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This unit was created to be the eyes and ears of the borough, monitoring pertinent real-time information to prevent unnecessary off-service issues.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Ambulances cannot respond to calls when they are back in the station restocking medicine or equipment.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So this unit observes resource levels in order to proactively restock when it is most efficient.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This unit also monitors hospital trends and timing, communicating with hospital personnel to understand where delays are occurring and resolving issues as they arrive.

chapters.summary: Esposito says FDNY is working with hospitals to reduce diversion and has asked hospital partners to add 911 ambulances, with three agreeing so far. He cites Staten Island hospitals agreeing to accept mental health patients and says FDNY invoked the state mutual aid agreement and welcomes volunteer units.
chapters.title: Esposito discusses hospital diversion and mutual aid efforts

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As with all areas of emergency response, the more communication and coordination between partners, the better the outcome.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've also been working with the Greater New York Hospital Association.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've asked our existing hospital partners who participate in the 911 system to add additional units.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: To date, three have agreed to provide additional assistance.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have also invoked our New York State Mutual Aid Agreement.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we continue to welcome units from the volunteer corps within the city to assist with 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: These are partners who are already familiar with our system and who have participated in past times of need, including during COVID.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've been working with the hospitals to address persistent diversion issues.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: One challenge that creates longer response times is when hospitals go on diversion and refuse to accept patients.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This is sometimes necessary for a variety of valid reasons.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But we also experience hospitals that frequently go on diversion for certain types of patients, which means that ambulances have longer trips to drop off patients and longer trips back to where they came from.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We continue to speak with hospitals where this practice creates persistent challenges to get them to go off diversion and become a destination for patients.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: One recent success is on Staten Island, where two hospitals that had consistently remained on diversion for mental health patients.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This in turn required ambulances to drive across the island to reach a hospital that was accepting that type of patient and then drive back across the island again to get back to the area it was serving.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: By these hospitals agreeing to begin accepting mental health patients, ambulances no longer need to traverse the island in order to transport patients to receive appropriate care.

chapters.summary: Esposito says FDNY is reviewing all EMS members in non-frontline positions and redeploying EMTs, paramedics, and officers to operational roles during lean staffing. He says two deputy chiefs were reassigned from offline positions to provide field guidance and supervision.
chapters.title: Esposito says FDNY is redeploying offline EMS members to the field

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've also done and are doing a full review of EMS members who are working offline who may be returned to the field.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We are currently reviewing all EMS members who do not work in frontline positions and redeploying to the field.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This includes emergency medical technicians, paramedics, and officers.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: A lot of EMS work happens in offline positions, including a lot of paperwork and analysis.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: However, during these times of lean staffing, we are transitioning as many members as possible back into operational roles.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: In particular, we have reassigned two deputy chiefs from offline positions to provide increased guidance and supervision to members.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: in the field.

chapters.summary: Esposito says FDNY is replacing its off-the-shelf scheduling program with a bespoke system and is testing artificial intelligence to improve ambulance deployment decisions. He says FDNY continues working with the Office of Technology and Innovation to update the EMS CAD system.
chapters.title: Esposito outlines long-term technology fixes for scheduling, AI, and CAD

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have also undertaken several long-term potential solutions.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: These are changes that require development before becoming fully operational, but they are steps that we are actively exploring or working on.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We are updating the digitized EMS schedule.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: FDNY's Bureau of Enterprise Technology is currently working to improve the daily scheduling program that we use for staff scheduling by replacing an off-the-shelf calendar program with

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: the bespoke product that we've built ourselves, the new scheduling system will be a better fit for our unique needs and operational requirements, enabling the department to more efficiently deploy resources.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We optimize deployment decisions through better technology.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We are testing ways that artificial intelligence technology can help us make more accurate decisions about deploying resources.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: While we currently make data-driven decisions to choose ambulance cross-street locations, we are exploring whether newer technology

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: can be helpful with those decisions, and whether they can be used in a balanced, safe way to yield better outcomes and help us reach patients faster.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As this committee is aware, we continue working with the City's Office of Technology and Innovation to update the EMS CAD system.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We expect that the new system will contain many tools that will improve the way we dispatch resources.

chapters.summary: Esposito discusses telemedicine, alternative transport, treat-in-place, and 911-to-988 programs as ways to avoid lengthy transports. He says callers overwhelmingly expect hospital transport, so these programs will require lengthy public education before significant use.
chapters.title: Esposito says alternate transport programs need public education

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: There are a variety of alternate ways to treat patients outside of the traditional model of transporting them to an emergency department at a hospital.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have piloted and tested different versions with varying levels of acceptance by the public.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Programs like telemedicine, alternative transport,

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Treat in Place and 911 to 988 provide models that would avoid lengthy transports.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: However, our experience has shown that the members of the public who call 911 are overwhelmingly expected to receive transport to a hospital.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So it will likely take lengthy periods of education and outreach before these programs are used by significant numbers of callers.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We continue to explore the appropriate method of pursuing these alternatives.

chapters.summary: Esposito says FDNY will work night and day to improve response times and appreciates the committee's attention. He says FDNY understands Intro 990's intent but believes the likely volume of notifications may not provide useful information, while remaining open to discussion.
chapters.title: Esposito says FDNY has much work left and raises concerns with Intro 990

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We know that we have a lot of work to do.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Addressing this challenge is something we will be working literally night and day to improve.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I know that rising response times is a concern for this committee as well, and I am appreciative of all of the attention that you've given to it.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Regarding Introduction 990, we understand and appreciate the intention of the bill.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As written, we don't believe that the likely volume of notifications that would result would necessarily provide useful information to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: However, we are open to further discussion and exploring ways to provide more real-time information to New Yorkers on this topic.

chapters.summary: Esposito says EMS had an incredibly busy year with code blue cold periods, FIFA World Cup visitors, America 250 events, and the International Naval Review. He praises EMS members for professionalism and life-saving work and offers to take questions.
chapters.title: Esposito praises EMS members after a busy year of events

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Before I conclude, I want to emphasize what a great job our members are doing despite this challenging environment.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This year was an incredibly busy year for EMS.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: In addition to the regular demands of the 911 system, we operated in circumstances that included extended code blue cold periods,

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: millions of visitors for the FIFA World Cup, numerous activities and events for the America 250 celebration and the International Naval Review, and we are preparing now for the holiday tourist season.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Our EMS members have risen to the challenge time after time, conducting themselves with professionalism, saving lives, and serving their fellow New Yorkers and visitors alike.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I am proud of the effort they make every day, and I am proud of the great success that they achieve, even in these most challenging circumstances.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We would be happy to take your questions at this time.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks why an ambulance never arrived for Jennifer Daly's son Kevin after he showed signs of a stroke. Esposito calls it unacceptable, and Chief Paul Miano says the 911 system was experiencing more than 100 extra calls; the call was classified as unknown and an ambulance arrived after the patient had already left for the hospital.
chapters.title: Ariola questions FDNY on ambulance no-show at St. Francis Prep

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just want to go and ask a few questions regarding the incident that took place at St.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Francis Preparatory High School that Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Daly testified to.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Going back to her testimony, Jennifer Daly noted that an ambulance never arrived for her child.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Who was showing signs of a stroke.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Can you explain why an ambulance did not arrive that day?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So before I defer to Chief Miano, we want to express our thoughts that it is unacceptable that we're not able to get an ambulance there in time.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As a parent, the thought that your child goes to school, has a medical emergency, it's recognized and they call for help.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It's unacceptable and we have to do better.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I'll pass it to Chief Miano and Chief Werner to describe the specific circumstances and what happened that day.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So echoing what Chief Esposito just said, this is a tragic incident that we, you know, want to try and stop from happening in the future.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: During the period of time where this call came in, EMD or the 911 system was experiencing an extreme number of calls, more than 100 calls than we normally receive during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Our call takers.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They don't just answer a phone and say, where's the address, and then dispatch out an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They spend a few minutes on the phone with each caller trying to ascertain exactly what is going on with that caller so we can dispatch the correct type of ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Unfortunately, during this time when the call was received, again, there were a high number of calls that came in, and our alarm receiving dispatches were on the phone with other callers.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: That does not mean that this call was not dispatched.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It was dispatched.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It was sent from our NYPD dispatcher over to the EMS dispatch, and it was put into the system.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It was classified as an unknown condition because we did not get to speak to the caller and triage the call ourself.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The call was dispatched out to an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The ambulance did start traveling towards the call, but the ambulance was coming from a distance, and it did take beyond.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The ambulance did arrive.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They arrived, unfortunately, after the patient left to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: At this point, I'm just going to pause questions because we've been joined by our speaker, Julie Menon, and she does have a statement that she would like to read.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin thanks the committees for holding a life-saving hearing and says New York City faces a crisis in its EMS teams. She says EMS responds to 1.6 million calls with only about 4,500 members, and low pay has led to attrition, recruitment problems, and workers living in shelters or cars.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin calls EMS understaffing and low pay a crisis

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Ariel, and I really want to thank you and the committee for holding this incredibly important, literally life-saving hearing today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I really wanted to come by, first of all, to say that we all know in the city that we are truly facing a crisis regarding our EMS teams who are obviously part of FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These teams save lives, yet they are understaffed and they are underpaid.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And this city council is very serious about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: These EMS teams, I don't need to overstate this, are truly saving lives every single day.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: They're responding to 1.6 million calls compared to FDNY's 500,000, yet they're only staffed by 4,500 members compared to FDNY's 13,000.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The average length of service for an emergency medical technician is just under three years because the pay of $18 an hour for hard, long work is simply untenable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So we are hearing story after story of our EMS workers, many of whom after their job are going and living in a shelter because they literally cannot afford housing or some are sleeping in their cars.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is truly unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I don't know what kind of city we are that we are.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: allowing this to continue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: The lack of adequate pay has obviously led to both rising attrition and low recruitment, which of course perpetuates this understaffing issue.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: With fewer staff, there are fewer ambulances ready to go at a moment's notice, which is obviously deepening the delays.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And when New Yorkers cannot rely on the emergency medical services to quickly respond to an emergency, who can they rely on?

chapters.summary: Menin describes a 16-year-old in her district who was badly hurt during a basketball game and received no EMS despite five separate 911 calls and a firehouse next door. She says a parent called a private ambulance after 30 minutes and FDNY called back nearly three hours later to ask if an ambulance was still needed.
chapters.title: Menin recounts basketball injury where five 911 calls brought no EMS

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Residents of my own district actually asked that very question recently, just a few days ago when a 16-year-old was badly hurt during a basketball game.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Despite five separate 9-11 calls, no EMS arrived.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Despite a firehouse actually being next door, no EMS arrived.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: 30 minutes after the first call, the teenager's parent contacted a private ambulance service because he couldn't wait any longer.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Nearly three hours after the first call, the FDNY phoned back to ask if an ambulance was still needed.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think, obviously, we're all relieved that his life was not at stake, but this is totally unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What if his life had been at stake?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This just cannot continue.

chapters.summary: Menin says the Mayor's Management Report shows an average response time of 13 minutes and 0.9 seconds, which she calls unacceptable. She notes brain cells begin to die after four minutes without oxygen and urges the city to pay EMS workers a living wage.
chapters.title: Menin cites 13:00.9 average response time and calls for living wage

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And there have been many cases where people's lives are literally on the line.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We've seen in the mayor's management report, the recent report came out, that the average response time is 13 minutes, 0.9 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: This is totally and wholly unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So as we wait for wages to increase, response times are increasing to truly unacceptable levels.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We know that brain cells begin to die after four minutes without oxygen.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So the idea that we are now at an average response time of 13 minutes, 0.9 seconds is just wholly unconscionable.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We must act now to pay those who provide the life-saving work a living wage and to ensure that New Yorkers in crisis can truly get the care they need.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So thank you, and I will now turn it over to Chair Areola for continued questioning.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks Speaker Menin and says the core issue is that EMS workers cannot survive on $18 an hour, leading to retention failures. She says the mayor's office must negotiate a competitive contract and not kick the can down the road.
chapters.title: Ariola agrees pay and retention are the crux of EMS crisis

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And you make a very valid point.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And it is the point that is at the crux of this issue is the fact that they cannot retain an EMS worker because they do not make enough money

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: to sustain themselves and have a family and support themselves.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And, yes, some live in shelters.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Some live.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: By the charity of family.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They cannot sustain themselves on $18 an hour and work three 12-hour shifts and then work a second or third job just to make ends meet.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So that's really the basis of the problem is

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You cannot retain and people will leave, whether it's to go to the fire department, to the DOT, to sanitation or to a private hospital.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So that's that's where we have to say that the mayor's office has to deal honestly and competitively with this.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: this contract that they are negotiating now with the unions, and not just kick the can down the road like previous administrations have.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They may not have caused this particular situation, but they certainly can end it.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And that's what we're looking forward to.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So thank you for bringing that up, Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That is really the crux of the problem.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I'd like to note that we've been joined by Councilmember Epstein.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And to the speaker's point of what happened with that particular incident in her district, I know that we've had conversation about that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'd like you to share the reason why an ambulance didn't come and then called three hours later to see if an ambulance came.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So before I give this to Chief Miano again, and this was a different reason than at St.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Francis Prep, but the idea that somebody, one of our children, can be hurt at a school and not get an ambulance in an acceptable amount of time.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But I've sat in front of the...

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: This committee several times with Fire Commissioner Bonsignor and before her Fire Commissioner Tucker, where we have said that the EMS system is in crisis.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And unfortunately, we're still in crisis.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we are working to improve this.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So for the specifics of that day, I'll pass it to Chief.

chapters.summary: Menin responds to FDNY testimony by saying the city council wants to raise wages but the administration and FDNY are the ones who can actually solve the crisis. She says she does not understand perpetuating the situation when lives are at risk.
chapters.title: Menin tells FDNY the administration must solve the EMS crisis

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just want to say, with all due respect, yes, you're saying it's in crisis, but you really are the only people who can solve the crisis.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, let's be clear.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You've got to be clear.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: city council that wants to raise the wages.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You all are the only people, the administration is the only people that can actually solve this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And I just, I don't understand how we can like keep perpetuating this when people's lives are literally at risk.

chapters.summary: Miano says the Wagner Middle School call was triaged as an injury, a lower-priority category, and several ambulances were dispatched. He says those ambulances were preempted and redirected to life-threatening emergencies, and fire engines are not dispatched to injuries.
chapters.title: Miano explains Wagner Middle School call and ambulance preemption

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So for that incident, that particular incident, that was called.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We did speak to the caller.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We did triage that call.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: That call was classified as an injury, which is a segment five category, and that is not considered a life-threatening emergency.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: An ambulance was dispatched.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Several ambulances actually were dispatched to respond to that call.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But while en route to that call, they were preempted and redirected to life-threatening emergencies that they were the closest ambulance to while they were responding to that assignment.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But when there's a firehouse next door, shouldn't there have been some?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I mean, I don't really understand where the breakdown in communication went in this situation where you've got three hours that this family is waiting.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So ambulances do not come out of firehouses.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But when you've got a situation where the ambulance are being rerouted, couldn't there have been an on-the-spot calculation to just check on this young boy?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So that the...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Fire engines are known as certified first responders, and there are certain call types that they respond to, and those are life-threatening emergencies like cardiac arrest, difficulty breathing, cardiacs with difficulty breathing.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Breathing.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They are not dispatched to injuries.

chapters.summary: Ariola returns to Kevin Daly's case and asks how often the system holds more than 100 calls and why critical calls are classified as unknown. Miano says call volume is up and staffing is down, and Werner explains the call came through the overflow position as an unknown condition because no call takers were available.
chapters.title: Ariola presses FDNY on unknown condition and calls on hold

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so just I will continue then with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So you said that you were holding 100 more, going back to Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Daly and her son Kevin and his issue.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So you were holding more than 100 calls, and it was put in as an unknown condition.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How often are you holding more than 100 calls, and how often do calls go into the system as unknown, especially when they are as critical as Kevin Daly's condition was?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I'll defer to Chief Warner to speak about how it's dispatched, why it was classified and unknown, and that process.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But as far as how many calls, how many times that we're holding calls, that many calls, unfortunately, that has risen over the last...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Over the last few years, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Our call volume is up, as Chief Esposito stated, and our head count is down, which means that we have less ambulances on the street to respond to those calls.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: However, our life-threatening, our most serious calls, our segment one through three assignments, cardiac arrest, difficulty breathing, shortness of breath, cardiaks, those do not hold.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Those calls are immediately dispatched out as soon as an ambulance is available.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Those are our most highest priority calls, and that is why the lower priority calls often

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: times while ambulances are responding to lower priority calls are redirected into more into higher priority calls because they are the closest ambulance and we do not want to have a situation where somebody who is in cardiac arrest is not receiving an ambulance

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: so i'm going to turn over to chief warner to explain the the the call typing and process and why it was designated as an unknown.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: So this call was processed by the overflow position, so we did not triage it.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: So the person that's categorizing it, giving it a call type, is relying on the information that PD obtained and relying on the code that they made it.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: So this call was designated as a 54Q, which translates in the EMS code to an unknown condition.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I would understand that if it was just the school nurse that was calling or the boy's mom, but a trained FDNY, a retired FDNY member called 911

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and stated clearly what was happening.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So what would a suspected stroke be?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: A segment one, three?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: What does that categorize as?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Had this call been triaged, it would have been categorized as a priority three.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Why wasn't it triaged?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: There were no call takers available at the time that this call came in.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether FDNY also has a low headcount for EMS dispatchers. Miano says EMS headcount includes everyone in the service, including field, dispatch, instructors, and medical affairs, so there is no specific separate headcount for dispatchers.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about EMS dispatcher headcount; Miano says no separate count

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So you also have a low head count for your EMS dispatchers as well?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So when we discuss EMS headcount, we're talking about every EMS employee that we have in the service.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And that includes members who ride on ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It includes the members who are in emergency medical dispatch.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It includes our instructors that are at training.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It also includes, you know, our people who work in Office of Medical Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: That includes every single EMT, paramedic, lieutenant, and officer that we have.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: There is no specific headcount for EMD, for the field, for training.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Our headcount is our headcount.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so you're telling me that a segment one, I'm going to expect a stroke to be a segment one, and I'm assuming a broken bone for you?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Segment three, maybe segment two, but neither of them were responded to.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: At least that parent got a call back.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Daly did not get a call back from EMS.

chapters.summary: Ariola says Intro 990 would let families know if an ambulance is not coming so they can make other arrangements sooner. Esposito says FDNY should continue discussing the issue but worries Notify NYC could confuse or frighten the public and discourage necessary calls.
chapters.title: Ariola defends Intro 990 as public notification of ambulance delays

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: This is why I had introduced Intro 990, which you testified to, Chief, that...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That you're open to further discussion, but you don't believe that likely volume notifications would result necessarily and provide useful information to New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
