utterances.text: I believe that if the speaker's constituents'parents were aware that an ambulance was not coming right away,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They would have chosen a different route earlier and called a private ambulance sooner.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And also the dailies would have done the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So that's why we have to do something so the public is aware, whether it's the bill, the intro as it stands, or if we work towards an amendment.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The public needs to know whether or not help is coming.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And I think we should continue discussion.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We just don't think that the NISM notification system is the correct way.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Our concern is that the public might be confused or fearful and then not call an ambulance when they really need one.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And in that situation, for those life-threatening calls, even if we're holding calls,

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: they get an ambulance while the lower acuity calls.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: In the case of the child at Wagner Middle School, that is not a life-threatening segment one, two, or three call.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So that's why they got preempted, those ambulances were preempted, and went to a life-threatening call.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But if the parents knew ahead of time, they would not have waited as long as they did.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I don't know how long they waited, but certainly I'm sure the child was at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Overall, it was an unacceptable wait time.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think the chair makes an excellent argument on this regard, is that families need to know if help is not coming.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Because if families knew help is not coming and we're going to be honest with you that you're not going to get an ambulance, then they would make other arrangements if they could, either a private ambulance or if someone is able to drive them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But just letting them sit there waiting and becoming more fearful and anxious and stressed and quite honestly, they're angry.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And they have every right to be angry.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We understand that, and we should work together to come up with a way to make sure that they are aware of that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We just don't think that that NISM alerting system is the correct way.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It's the correct way to alert everyone for everything.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I don't know why it wouldn't pertain here.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But we're also open to discussion on it.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks how EMS call takers are scheduled and what number of held calls the system can safely handle. Miano says call takers are staggered based on historical volumes, and he explains that the system prioritizes high-acuity calls and redirects ambulances rather than using a fixed safe hold number.
chapters.title: Ariola asks call taker staffing and safe hold numbers

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So how?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How often and what are the number of EMS call takers that EMS call takers are available?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So EMS call takers are scheduled in a staggered.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They report in a staggered manner throughout the day based on historical call volume highs and lows.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So at our peak time, we are staffed with the peak amount of call takers that we have.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: In our off-peak times, we work on staggering up and staggering down.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But I will defer to Chief Werner for more clarification.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Our baseline schedule is a three, eight and a half hour shift around the clock.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: And then I stagger the 12 hour members throughout the day into the evening when our call volume increases.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For lack of a better word, what, in your opinion, is the safe amount of calls to be on hold that the system can handle in the current staffing state?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Could you just repeat that one more time?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So what do you believe is a safe amount of calls to be on hold in the system that the system now can handle in its current staffing state?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: 200 calls, 100 call.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Like if you get an average of 100 calls in a day, and I'm making that number up, and now you've got 200 calls that day, what's the breaking point?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I think it's...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It's much more dynamic than it being so black and white to be able to just come out with a number, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: 38% of the calls that we receive every day are what we consider to be high acuity or life-threatening.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So that means the other 62% calls that come in are not considered life-threatening or high priority.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we do not want our life-threatening.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: assignments to hold at all.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And that is why the system is designed where if we are responding to a low acuity assignment, an ambulance is redirected to a higher acuity assignment.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So there is no number, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: There's no exact number that I could give you that would make any sense because it varies so much, not just day to day, but hour to hour and literally moment to moment.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Like I mentioned to the speaker, we had several ambulances responding to the

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: constituent's injury, but they were redirected because someone else called and they were having what is considered a life-threatening emergency.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks for the average number of calls on hold. Miano says the number is too dynamic to reduce to a single figure because it varies hour to hour and moment to moment, and the system holds lower-acuity calls while responding to life-threatening emergencies.
chapters.title: Miano says average calls on hold varies moment to moment

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: What is the average number of calls on hold?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Again, it's not that I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It's just that it varies, literally varies from moment to moment.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: If we have high acuity calls coming in, they're not holding, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But if we have an enormous amount of high acuity calls coming in and at the same time

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: low acuity calls, we need to ensure the high acuity life-threatening emergencies are responded to and we may need to hold

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: someone who is called up because they have an illness or an injury that does not meet the life-threatening criteria.

chapters.summary: Ariola notes Kevin Daly's case was life-threatening but went into the system as unknown after four calls. Miano says FDNY disputed none of that and reviewed the assignment minute by minute, and Werner says they are improving communications between NYPD and EMS.
chapters.title: Ariola asks how to prevent another Kevin Daly incident

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so, but Kevin Daly was a life-threatening call, and four calls were placed, and he went into unknown conditions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So how can we prevent an incident like that from happening in the future?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So what you just stated was 100% correct, and we are not disputing that, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So what Chief Werner, and again, Chief Werner, I'll defer to her to speak on it, but as soon as this came to our attention, right, we

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: painstakingly went through every single line of the assignment, minute to minute to minute, all the calls that were made, all of the interactions between the police dispatchers and the EMS dispatchers, and then

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: our radio dispatchers to see was there a unit available, where were they responding from.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And we are working on improving our communications between NYPD and EMS.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Chief Werner?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: That's very accurate.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: We are looking to improve the communications between PD and EMS to make sure that we get vital information.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was the second part of the question?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How can we make it better?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: How can we make sure that incidents like this don't happen in the future?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Currently, I'm utilizing, I have offline members as well doing other functions such as QA and training.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: So during periods of high call volume, I am putting them offline and bringing them, taking them offline and bringing them to the call-taking floor to increase our capacity.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks how often mutual aid is used and when hospitals can divert certain ambulance patients. Miano says volunteer agencies help when available, while hospital diversions are evaluated by an EMS officer and may be limited to certain patient types or services.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about mutual aid and hospital diversion rules

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So what is the current status of the supplemental tours via mutual aid?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: In your testimony, you said you're utilizing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So how often are you utilizing?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Only when needed, or are they available at all times?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we put a request out to all the volunteer agencies that operate in New York City, and they are volunteers.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So they don't commit to us on certain dates and times, but when they are able to log in and put a unit into the system, we log them into the system and they help us.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We do have some volunteer agencies that are tremendous and are consistently running units like our Central Park volunteers.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: You know, we very consistently can count on Central Park volunteers to be in service and available and handling calls that occur within that Central Park area.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And in what circumstances can a hospital divert certain types of ambulance patients?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So when a hospital requests a diversion, we send an EMS officer over to evaluate what is going on over at the hospital and the reason why they need to do.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And there are many reasons why a hospital can ask for a diversion.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It could be a utilities or infrastructure issue, such as power outage, computer IT issues.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It could also be that there are certain types of monitoring that needs to be done on certain types of patients.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So they could divert for cardiac patients because they have no more beds that have monitors.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Perhaps they can divert for a stroke patient because their CAT scan is not working.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we work, as soon as a hospital advises us that they need to go on a diversion, we send an officer to evaluate what's going on, and we speak with the administrator on duty.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We also involve our Office of Medical Affairs.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Excuse me, to determine, you know, how long that this diversion and whether it needs to be a complete and total diversion, or do we just need to divert certain areas or certain patients that we are taking to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Because maybe the general emergency room is open and operating, but L&D is having an issue.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we would keep the hospital open for general emergency, but we wouldn't transport someone who is having a baby.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks about engine companies responding to medical emergencies, including a firehouse near the school in the speaker's example. Esposito says CFR engine companies are assigned only to segment one, two, or three life-threatening calls; they cannot transport and are not sent to lower-acuity injuries.
chapters.title: Ariola asks when fire engines are dispatched to medical calls

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, and the speaker noted that there was an engine company right next door to the school.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So in what's...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Circumstances, are engine companies dispatched to a medical emergency?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So our engine companies, the firefighters there are certified first responders with defibrillation capability.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They are assigned in segment one, two, and three calls.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: All of our medical calls, when they hit the emergency medical dispatcher, get triaged and get a segment.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So if it's a segment one, two, or three, which we see as the life-threatening calls, that CFR engine, if available, will be assigned.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: In the case that the speaker was talking about, that was a segment four or five, and the CFR engine is not, which cannot transport, is not assigned to those.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Has the FDMY ever explored the utility of having certain members of fire companies undergo training as EMTs and paramedics, those who did not come into the fire department through that pipeline?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I guess in years past, they were things they...

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The possibility was looked at.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've had thousands of our members over the last 25 or 30 years that came from EMS that were either EMTs or paramedics.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But the way we look at it now is that the EMTs and paramedics are on the ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Which is not optimal, right?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We want ambulances to go to ambulance calls.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So what is the process of getting an engine company back in service after responding to a medical call?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And does the company have to wait until an ambulance arrives?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Yes, once that CFR engine makes patient contact, they are required to wait for an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we've had times where that engine, because it winds up being a lower acuity call, could wait an hour or two with the patient waiting for an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The engine is not able to transport, and they are not able to leave the patient.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They cannot abandon that patient, regardless of the level of illness or injury.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: While the engine company is at the scene of a medical call.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That fire call would be handled by other fire companies.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That fire company cannot leave.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So what we're seeing is when a fire engine has to respond, there's gaps for possible fires that are happening in their district, in the area that they cover, their catchment area.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Then they have to call in another fire engine company, and that leaves another gap.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So you see what's happening here.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It's just it's...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It puts more people in danger and it creates more of a public safety issue.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just want to mention also we've been joined by Council Members Gail Brewer and Lincoln Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just have a couple more questions and then I will defer to Chair Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Miano explains that ALS ambulances are staffed by paramedics who can provide advanced cardiac care, medications, and airway management, while BLS ambulances are staffed by EMTs. He describes paramedics as bringing the emergency room to the patient.
chapters.title: Miano explains ALS and BLS ambulance staffing and roles

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Just for those who don't understand, could you please explain the roles of personnel on ALS and BLS ambulances?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So an ALS ambulance is advanced life support that's staffed by paramedics, and BLS ambulances are staffed by EMTs, which is BLS stands for basic life support.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So paramedics, I'm sorry, so I'll expand a little more, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Paramedics can provide advanced cardiac life support.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They can provide medications that basic life support cannot.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They can provide advanced airway maneuvers like endotracheal intubation to secure somebody's airway who's not breathing.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So the paramedics...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Are an advanced level of care that provide additional medications almost.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We're an emergency room on wheels, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We bring the emergency room to your home, to the scene that you call, whether it's on the street, in your home.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And our medics, our paramedics, and the paramedics that operate in the 911 system, whether FDNY or anyone who operates in the 911 system, they are...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it goes with the name, when New York City's best.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And when they come out and they assess the situation and they acknowledge the fact that this is a life-threatening situation, they go to work.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And this is the only emergency agency whose primary goal, their only goal, is life.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And that is what they do every single day.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And they put their own lives on the line to ensure that other people can reunite with their families and go home and not just save lives, but bring lives into the world.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: There's no better feeling.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Than going from a cardiac

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: arrest save to a couple hours later delivering a baby.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Who gets to experience and do that in the same day?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Only the members of New York City's EMS system.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And that is why we have to do everything that you've stated up here, that you've stated in your opening testimony, that the chief of department has stated, that the speaker has stated.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We have to take care of New York City's best.

chapters.summary: Ariola reiterates the need for a living wage and uniformed first responder status, then asks whether two paramedics are needed for ALS and what happens if staffing is low. Miano says two paramedics are needed for effective advanced life support, and Esposito says fire companies must stay with patients until an ambulance arrives.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about two-paramedic staffing and fire company scene time

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yes, in many ways.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I will say it again.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It begins with a living wage for EMS and paramedics, because then we will not have a retention problem.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We will not have a nutrition problem, and they will be getting paid.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: To compensate them for the job that they do because they are saving lives.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They don't even have, and most people don't know this, they don't even have uniformed first responder status.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They're categorized as civilians.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So we need to really sit, and we will hear from the unions later, but I know that I've asked for FDNY to leave someone behind, and I know that the mayor's office is here,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: a representative, because that is an area where really, if we can fix that,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We can then work on all the other problems, and we need to do that right away.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Does the fire department believe that two paramedics are needed for ALS?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And if so,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So who's driving the ambulance?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So two paramedics are needed to provide effective advanced life support care.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: In our training, right, we train as a team.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We don't train as individuals.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: As an RN, as a nurse, you know that prior to the delivery of medication, I don't just look at that medication.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: My partner has to look at that medication, confirm I'm giving the correct medication, confirm the dose is correct, confirm the route is correct.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So that is why two people with the same level of care need to be in the back of an ambulance and treating patients with life-threatening emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So in situations where both paramedics need to be in the back of an ambulance, a BLS ambulance does respond, and they drive that vehicle, both vehicles, while the two paramedics are operating in the back.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, and just to round out, would one EMT and one paramedic be able to provide the needed care?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And does the FDMY believe that fire companies should stay on scene for non-acute calls?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I'll take the first part of it.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And there are extreme situations where we have multiple patients, right, on the scene, and we need to split up.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We need to divide and conquer.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We do duplicate the amount of equipment on an ambulance so two paramedics can handle two patients.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And, you know, in those situations or in a fire or a bad car accident or even an incident, maybe it's a carbon monoxide incident.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: in a home where there's multiple patients who are unresponsive, we will divide both of those two paramedics up so they can operate.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But it is not optimal to operate as a sole paramedic in the back of an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But with staffing so low,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I think that's something that you should do since it was done during COVID and it can be done.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We are in a state of emergency right now with ambulances, and that's why we spoke about, we had a meeting with the mayor's office about mutual aid, about bringing everybody off the desk and into the ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So in a state of emergency, I think that that might be something you'd want to look at.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Chair, respectfully, I don't know who advised that we did that during COVID, but that was not a step that we took during COVID.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It may have been on our...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: You know, our list of considerations, but it was not something that we transitioned to during COVID.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And to your question about the point of a fire company staying with the patient, we believe that when there's a patient that needs an ambulance, we have to stay with them to ensure that they don't get any worse.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I yield now to Chair Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about the engine company near a school and whether it could rush a child to the hospital. Esposito says the engine was not assigned because the call was not life-threatening, and even if sent it could not transport and would be tied to the scene.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks why nearby engine could not transport injured child

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I heard about the engine, like, that was next to where the school, not too far.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So what are the steps someone can take, like, in the case of an emergency?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Like, you can't, the engine cannot call and say this is an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Let's say if there's a rotation, they can call and say that there is an emergency here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: One of us got to run with the child.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: In that case where engine 44 is, if they, because it's not a life-threatening call, the engine doesn't get assigned.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Once we was to send them there, even to confirm, but...

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Then they would be tied to that scene and they're not able to transport that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That child needed transportation to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The engine's not able to do that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So they would just be waiting there, and that's why we reserve them for the serious life-threatening calls so they can provide life-saving care until that ambulance gets there.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: There's not much that engine could have done for that boy with the broken leg.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Narcisse agrees with Ariola that retention is a problem rooted in inadequate pay, saying EMS workers leave for nursing or other jobs. She also says the city must educate residents not to call 911 for non-emergencies and discusses how lack of insurance drives emergency room use.
chapters.title: Narcisse links retention to pay and 911 misuse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm in agreement with the chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Retention is a problem.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And when I spoke, I was at Garrison Beach, the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: and so on.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And one of the things is just the pay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The pay is not right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: People are not going to stay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They're going to go to nursing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They're going to go do something else.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we have to look into that seriously.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And another thing, which I want to introduce a bill on that, it's...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's calling 911.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We are in a habit everywhere we go, even police department, people in the meeting will tell you, oh, emergency, call 911.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We're not detailing anything, and that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And another problem that we're facing right now, it's folks losing their insurance, and they end up in an emergency room.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And they will call 911 because they know they can get in faster.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And as a nurse, I'm going to tell you, I know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Some of them will tell you they have respiratory problems just to get in an ambulance and to get to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All those cultures, we have to be in together.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I hope people are hearing me.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Stop calling 911 if you don't have to.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You can actually get in the hospital because sometimes the ambulance come waiting.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And by the time I do a triage, I realize that patient is not an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: There is no reason that patient should be calling 911.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But how do you say that?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You just have to be patient because they told people if you have any problem.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The person have a chronic illness, emphysema, and they're still calling 911 even though they have medication.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's a problem that we have to work on our own culture in the city of New York to try to decrease it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But retention is a must.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks H&H about current emergency department wait times and the time to transfer admitted patients to inpatient beds. Dr. Josh Motzquist says the median time to first provider is 29 minutes and the average emergency department-to-bed time is about 270 minutes.
chapters.title: Narcisse questions H&H on emergency department and bed transfer waits

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now, going to H&H.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What are the current average emergency department wait times for H&H citywide?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And how do we compare to the past two years?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Narcis.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It's good to see you again, and I appreciate all you do for hospitals and helping us.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: The current median arrival time to seeing the first provider is 29 minutes in health and hospitals overall, which is an improvement from previous years of 33 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How long does it take on average for a patient to be transferred from the emergency department to the inpatient hospital bed?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: One of the measures we try to track is after the decision is made to admit the patient, how long it takes to get out of the emergency department to bed upstairs.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: To the bed.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And right now that time is on average about 270 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: 270 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I was hoping for 70.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We would all for 70.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm just hopeful.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And what do you think is a problem?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I think it's a complex situation.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It depends on what the capacity of the facility is at the time of day, what time of day it is, what resources are available.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It depends how many patients are coming in, how many are being admitted.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Also, getting patients home is also a challenge sometimes, getting patients out the door.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: There's a lot of different variables that kind of contribute.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I know there's a lot of different factors.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can you give me the top one?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: The top one, I don't have the top one in front of me.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I'm happy to get that back to you.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: But a combination of getting patients out of the hospital and getting patients upstairs all contribute to the overcrowding nature.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether wait times vary by hospital and which H&H hospitals have the longest and shortest waits. Motzquist says he does not have all hospital-level data but notes variation by time of day, capacity, admissions, and discharges, and cites Lincoln Hospital as seeing about 37 patients per hour at peak.
chapters.title: Motzquist says wait times vary by hospital and factors

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do wait times vary by hospital?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If so, which hospital report the highest and the lowest wait times?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I don't have the wait times of all the hospitals in the city with us here today.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: You know, I could say that in the city, H&H, I'm always running through there, at least.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I don't know if I have the H&H data, but I can get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I could say that it depends on several factors.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: You know, time of day matters a big difference, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Sometimes people come in.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Depends on whether a mass casualty incident occurs, as the chief had mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: depends on the seasonality as well.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: You know, as flu season comes through, people get sicker with different illnesses.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: There's lots of different variables that contribute to it, and we try to staff to demand to meet those expectations.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: There's a lot of variables, but what I'm getting to, trying to, is to see what are the top one and what's the plan to make it better.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because right now we're in a crisis.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It is a real crisis for us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Which H&H hospital currently experienced the longest emergency department wait times and what factors are driving those delays?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I don't have the number of the longest in front of me, but I can say a certain facility like Lincoln sees about 37 patients per hour arriving at any given moment at its peak.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so when a patient's arriving literally more than one every two minutes, it's a lot of volume coming in for them to manage, and we have to increase staffing and increase our resources to meet those needs.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about emergency room staffing and whether provider-in-triage models have been sustained. Motzquist says staffing is variable and facilities use different models; provider-in-triage can speed initial care but does not always improve throughput.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about ER staffing and provider-in-triage model

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How are we doing with staffing in the ER?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because ER is important.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If you don't get the patient to be seen in, they're not going to go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I hope there's no shortage there.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: You know, we could always use more resources, but staffing is important, and it's variable.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We have, you know, physicians, nurses, patient care techs.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I'm only naming just a few of the needs of our emergency departments.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: As you know, we're a complex, like a Formula One team.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We all have different roles and responsibilities to address a patient in crisis.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And when a critically ill patient comes in, a mass casualty, we have a lot of trauma centers.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: A trauma patient comes in, a whole lot of resources have to get consumed in that patient for.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Quite some time sometimes to stabilize and save that person's life.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: H&H previously reported that provider in triage models reduced time to provider at Lincoln Hospital by approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Have those improvements been sustained and have similar models been implemented successfully at other facilities?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Some of our facilities use a provider and triage model, and what that does is allow the physician or physician associate to see the patient sooner and start the care sooner.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It doesn't necessarily always improve the throughput of the case there, and so we have to kind of vary and see what the value is of putting a provider up front versus being there throughout the entire patient experience.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks where patients await inpatient beds and how H&H handles space constraints and hallway crowding. Motzquist says it is facility-specific, that ideally no patient waits in hallways, but H&H will use hallway and other spaces when necessary.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks where patients wait and about hallway crowding

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Where are patients awaiting transfer from the emergency department to inpatient bed typically held?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was that question?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Where the patient usually, where you keep the patient after you finish in the ER to transfer to go to the bed.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I think it's a very facility-specific question and depends.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Some facilities try to designate a separate space in the emergency department for it.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Some use a scattered approach.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so it's very facility dependent on how they manage those operations.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Some is constrained by building construction and resource availability.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so I wouldn't be able to answer that question off the top of my cuff.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How are we doing with the space-wise?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because one of the problems that we face in many ERs that we don't have no space at all.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We end up putting a bunch of folks in the hallway and become more chaotic.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are we doing well in that setting?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I mean, that's a hard question to answer, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So ideally, we never put any patients in the hallway.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Ideally, you would never have that need, but we will always see patients when they come in.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We try to see them as soon as possible, and we'll use any available resource we have available for that, including hallway spaces and other areas.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because that delayed the process too, you know that, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I said that delayed the process.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: When you have people overcrowded here.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Absolutely, it makes it more challenging.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What impact do prolonged emergency department and inpatient bed wait times have on patient outcomes, quality of care, and hospital operations?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you one more time, please?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What impact do prolonged emergency department and inpatient bed wait times have on patients'outcomes, quality of care, and hospital operations?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I've seen some mixed studies on that.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I think overall we feel that the sooner the patient gets up to an inpatient bed, it's better for the patient.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I think it's more humane and private and decent for them to be there, and the resources are better served.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so we strive in our limited resource environment to do the best possible we can with the resources we have.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The reason I've been asking all those questions, you know, I lived it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And one of the things, the patient get aggravated for staying in the ER, in the hallway for a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And that actually get them frustrated.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That when you stress, you know, your quality of care, the things that are in your mind, the confidence that you have in, you know, the trust, everything just become a ripple effect.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I think we have to assess our emergency space as well.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Patients might get the impression they're not being cared for, for example, but they are being cared for, even though in situations.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We've seen episodes of violence increase in the emergency department.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We've seen nurses attacked, physicians attacked, EMS attacked.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: People forget.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Because when you're in this environment where you're ill and you're not getting better and you're stressed and breached, it's very complicated and very challenging for them.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Absolutely.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about patients leaving against medical advice and the most common reasons for emergency visits. Motzquist says left-without-being-seen data is around 2%, common complaints include chest pain, belly pain, and shortness of breath, and mental health calls are complex with B-HEARD and 988 partnerships.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about AMA rates, common ER visits, and mental health

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And that's why sometimes they sign against the medical advice and walk out.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many, by example, how many of our patients actually get in the emergency room and did not finish getting care and sign against medical advice?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you have that data?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I don't have the AMA data with us, and I'm happy to get it for you.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I know that our left without being seen data is around 2% in general.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: About 2%?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What are the most common reasons people visit emergency rooms?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you track them to assess the need to continue improving services?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yes, and every facility is going to have a little differences, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: A little different nuances to what their patient population comes to.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: In general, patients come in for chest pain, come in for belly pain, come in for, you know, shortness of breath.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Under EMTALA, we take care of any patients that come in, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so when an individual layperson might perceive to be an emergency, we're here to help them and figure out whether it is a true life-threatening emergency or not and try to care for them as best of our ability.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we track it in the year.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We ask people what they come after the triage nurse finished.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have a data that we enter it to say why that person is here.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So that data should be easy to gain because the nurses have to tell you why from the triage nurse, why that person was here specifically.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What was the main complaint?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yes, and each facility has slightly different chief complaints that are their priority.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I don't have the data in front of me, but we can break it down for you if you'd like us to.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What are you assuring New Yorkers with mental health needs are being taken to the correct facilities instead of the emergency room?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How can we streamline this process?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: That is a complicated question.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm prepared to answer today.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Mental health crises are really important.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I know that the 911 system is central to the BHERDS operation that we're working with, and that we are continuing to work closely with both FDNY and NYPD to address any operational challenges for the mental health crisis system,

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: and improving call triage, working with agency partners to drive mental health calls to 988 as an example.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Other behavioral health services can reduce unnecessary strain on emergency resources to make sure that New Yorkers who are experiencing mental health crises receive the most appropriate response.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you're doing some kind of education too as well for those patients?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Let's say a patient come in and they have mental health, like it's not really an emergency acute to be in an emergency room.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So do we use that opportunity?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I used to tell the patient, these are the information and kind of guide the patient through the next step.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We try to provide patients with the appropriate resources to help them get the care they need.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And you talk very kind of a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I apologize for that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want everybody to be able to hear the answer.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether H&H has seen increased emergency department volume or hospital admissions. Motzquist says volume has been increasing since 2020, with over 1.1 million emergency department patients across 11 facilities in 2025, and higher-acuity cases have increased significantly.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks H&H about emergency volume and acuity increases

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Challenges that we have.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Have H&H Hospital experienced an overall increase in emergency department volume or hospital admission in recent years?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yes, let me just get the data, please.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: The overall emergency volume has been increasing since 2020.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Our volume is...

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I apologize, I don't have the data.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Our 2025 eating counters are over 1 million patients.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Over 1 million emergency department patients across our 11 facilities, 1.1 million in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: The biggest increase for us has also been in the higher acuity cases.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So we try to rank our patients by severity index.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: You might be familiar with the ESI scoring, if you remember back in the day, the emergency service index.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so one through five, one tends to be a sicker patient, five tends to be a less sick patient.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And our overall increase in the ones and twos have significantly increased over time.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says many problems require educating patients on preventive care and connecting them to clinics and community resources. Motzquist agrees and describes spending much of his clinical time educating patients about their diseases and appropriate care options.
chapters.title: Narcisse presses H&H on education and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Most of the question.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Sure, no problem.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Most of the question that I'm asking is just, I think it has to do with a lot of education.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have to educate people wherever we can get them and then to decrease for people to have a better understanding and to focus on preventive care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you have a lot of...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: clinics, different places that we can redirect people.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I think engagement with the community, how involved are you in the community to help decrease those processes?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because wherever you can get people, you have to meet them where they are.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And are we doing that in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: That's absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: As a practicing emergency physician, I spend a lot of my day with my patients just educating them about, A, their disease, but also how to take care of the disease, how to find the right resources, how to get the care they need, and where the most appropriate place for that care is.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: A lot of my day is spent connecting those dots and really just encouraging them to take good care and prevent this illness from occurring.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I had a recent case where a woman was very ill from sepsis.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: because she didn't understand how to get to the doctor in time, to get the antibiotics in time, to get the care, what resources were available, and she waited too long before she came to see me.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And it was very sad and very tragic.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so I think a large part of our care is connecting the dots of the resources, which are sometimes complicated and complex for patients to navigate, and we do the very best to try to provide those resources to our patients.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are you closing any clinics?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I'm not aware.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Outpatient clinics?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do we have?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are we?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because if folks don't have insurances, I'm concerned that they will get, you know, toward the ER.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So are we doing?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we're not talking about preventive care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: This is part of the plan of preventive care.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I mean, as health and hospitals, our goal is to strive to help.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Preventative is the best, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We strive to help every New Yorker, regardless of means, ability, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so our goal is to take care of anyone who comes for care.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And I'm not aware of any clinics being closed.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I can find out if that's the case or not.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: But we have, you know, in the example, financial counselors who enroll our patients in New York City care.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: To help get them preventive medicine, primary care.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We have a virtual express care as an example where we connect patients online through telephonic, through video calls to give them care on the spot.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether patient needs have become more acute or complex and what operational challenges contribute to long waits. Motzquist says care is increasingly complex, with laboratory, imaging, and medication processes adding time, especially at high-volume facilities.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about complex patient needs and ER operational challenges

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Within the last several years, have patient needs become more acute or complex?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And has that affected emergency department throughout in the wait times?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I would say over the course of my career, I've seen a lot of complexities of care.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: The drugs are changing, the pathology is changing, our knowledge is changing, and so all of it's becoming more difficult to navigate.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Connecting patients to resources is always challenging, and I think the more options and the more needs will always make that more difficult.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What are the primary operational challenges contributing to Pulong Emergency Department wait times?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm coming back to that again.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah, I know.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, when you think about a patient who comes to the emergency department, there's so many needs they have, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So whether that patient needs laboratory assessment, whether they need radiographic assessment, whether they need medication administration, all those things take time.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: The time it takes to draw blood, send it to a lab, get results back, all these things add up.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And depending on the complexity, they keep multiplying, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It's not just a one-plus-one scenario.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And you add that with the fact that a facility that gets 37 patients an hour trying to accommodate that many patients at once also makes it more complicated and complex.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Have you...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Think about exploring having those clinics closer to the hospital where you see the emergencies coming all the time that don't need, because I know you have the data.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You just have to go back to triage to see what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So if all the, like let's say if it's mental, so maybe we can anticipate partnering or having a place where you're not putting it and then you can move people out of the emergency room a little faster.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I mean, part of the issue is...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You don't need transportation because we already have problems with...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I mean, EMS, you know, to come and get those patients.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, so I mean, part of it is we do have clinics in our facilities as well.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: But under the federal EMTALA laws, we have to do an emergency treatment and screening exam for all patients that present, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And a lot of times in some of these lower QD patients, by the time I'm done with my EMTALA screening exam, I can pretty much diagnose you and send you on the way.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so simply diverting them to another clinic isn't always the right answer, but educating them on the opportunities available next time instead of presenting to the emergency department might give that option.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So as I said before, a lot of my time is educating the public on what options do exist, how to search for help, how to ask for help, and what other resources might exist for health care besides the emergency department.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm going to ask one more question, and I'm going to try to get it back to chair because I have a lot of questions more that we, because today is about what can we do together

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: that we can decrease the wait time in the ER and how fast our...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: EMS can get to the patient.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: FDNY is helping us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We're just looking for solutions to the problem we're facing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And that's the reason I'm going to come back for more questions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'll ask you the last one, and I'll come back again.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what strategies H&H is pursuing to reduce overcrowding and shorten wait times. Motzquist cites virtual express care, where some 911 calls are transferred to H&H for virtual evaluation and treatment, sometimes diverting an ambulance from being dispatched.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about strategies to reduce overcrowding; virtual express care

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What specific strategies is H&H pursuing to reduce overcrowding, improve patients'flow, and shorten?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: With times.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, so one of the strategies we have done and we've partnered with FDNY on is virtual express care as an example.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so we will see patients virtually over phone or video.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so some 911 calls are being transferred to our virtual express care calls.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: and allowing us to treat on the spot right there and sometimes divert an ambulance from even being dispatched to that facility, to that person as well.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you have your mobile unit.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: My understanding is just...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If a patient, because one of the things that we lack of doing, telling the patient, open visit, in the clinics as well as in the hospital, do not call 911.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: This is the step you need to take.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I think that's one of the bills I'm looking to see how shaping we started already, to see what can we do to help those folks in terms of education, not pressure.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because sometimes it's a simple education you give people, they can do better.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: If we can be reinforcing it, if we just say it and then you move on, people forget.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Maybe we can see if we can get, you know, advertisement somewhere, a spot, something going on and using social media, educating people.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we need to educate people and reinforce it so at least we can decrease the flow of people and then we don't want to lose lives in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I'm going to pass it on by my chair and then probably opening up for some colleagues'questions and I'll come back.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Can I just say, Chair, thank you so much for that.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I mean, the emergency department is the safety net of this country, right, and of the city.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And patients know they can always come to us, be seen.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We will never turn you away.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And that's why I love my job and I love doing the work that I do is because we will always take care of patients who show up.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: But the challenge is exactly what you discussed.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: And so I think there might be opportunity for us to discuss.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Later, look forward to seeing that bill.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Where can we decrease or redirect patients to find the most appropriate care they need?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I really believe in preventative care, and that's what I've been preaching, and it seems like it's a slow motion right now, and we need to sit down and collaborate, whatever we can do here with my colleagues to structure it to help and make it happen.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I look forward to the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: After Ariola yields to members, Council Member Vickie Paladino says the council fought for EMS pay parity in the fiscal 2027 budget and warned about losing experienced personnel. She asks how many ambulance tours are out of service; Miano says the system averages over 90 off-service ambulances per day, overwhelmingly due to staffing.
chapters.title: Paladino presses for EMS pay parity and asks about out-of-service ambulances

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yes, we will yield now to Council Members Shulman, then Brooks-Powers, then Epstein, Palladino, and Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Can I yield to Palladino because she has to leave?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Most certainly.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: First off, let me say this.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We have fought very hard for pay parity for the EMS workers.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: It was one of our top priorities for the fiscal budget of 27.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We raised this issue repeatedly during the delegation meetings, formally submitted it as part of our budget priorities, and pleaded with the Finance Department to address the compensation disparity.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We warned that if EMS workers were not paid the wages that they deserve, the city would continue to lose experienced personnel to better-paying jobs, making it increasingly difficult to maintain

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: adequate staffing, and timely emergency responses.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we are now seeing the consequences of those concerns.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: EMS workers are being overwhelmed by call volume, and response times are increasing.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: This is not simply a workforce issue.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: It is a public safety issue.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: New Yorkers are calling 911.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Should they not wonder whether or not an ambulance will arrive when they need it?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Our EMS workers provide life-saving care every day, often under extraordinary demanding conditions.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: They deserve fair compensation, and the city must treat EMS staffing and pay parity as a public safety priority that they indeed are.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You know, we're listening to you guys get kind of crucified here at the whys and how comes and what fors.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: When you receive the amount of calls that you receive every single day, and you do not have the amount of

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: emergency vehicles that you need to respond, nor do you have the personnel that you need to respond to these calls, everybody's sitting here and wondering, why?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: How come?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Well, we need more people.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We need to hire the people to do these jobs.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: They're moving on because their pay is not significant.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: The speaker came in, and that's the first thing she rattled off, and she's 100% right.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: I'd like to know, on an average, how many ambulance tours are out of service at any time?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: What are the reasons that the ambulance might be out of service?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So in a 24-hour period, we're averaging over 90 ambulances off service per day, and that is overwhelmingly due to staffing.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Staffing.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Again, staffing.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Not enough people to sit in the cars, in the emergency vehicles, and take them where they're needed.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So would you say that...

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: At least 85% of what you heard here today, had this budget

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: been met to your needs and you were funded as you should have been funded, would you say some of these problems would not even be existing today?

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Because you would be able to get to point A to point B to point C in a timely fashion.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We believe that solving the pay issue is the first step to getting everything back on track.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So this $126 billion budget that this city passed, none of it went to you.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And what you guys actually need to do your jobs so that the people, that young kid at St.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Francis Prep,

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And to the speaker's point, the emergency that she faced, your ambulances would have been able to get there in a timely fashion had they been staffed properly and if these people were paid properly.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We could never make a guarantee, but we don't think we'd be holding calls as frequently as we are now.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: So once again, I call upon New York City's Budget Committee and New York City's mayor, and I want to know why the funds are not appropriated as to where they should be appropriated to.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: We are facing a public safety issue here, and you guys are on the front line, and you're sitting here at a dais today being asked all these questions that basically can be fixed.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: You know, there's problems, but there's solutions to every single problem that this city is facing.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: And all we need to do is put the money where the money belongs.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Vickie Paladino
utterances.text: That's all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Councilmember Shulman, the gracious Councilmember Shulman.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lynn Schulman notes she is the only council member who worked for EMS and asks whether response time is measured point-to-point. Miano says response time is calculated from the 911 call until the ambulance arrives on the scene, not until providers reach the patient.
chapters.title: Shulman asks how FDNY defines response time

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: First of all, I want to say that I am the only member of the City Council that used to work for the Emergency Medical Service.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: On the leadership side, I know a lot of the people that are sitting here in the audience today.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The issue of pay parity has been a longstanding issue, and I was there many, many years ago.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And so, you know, so I have some questions.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: One is, so, Chief, you said in your remarks that you're in the midst of a promotional cycle.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That promotional cycle has so many EMTs in it because of the pay issue.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Or a large part of it is the pay issue.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
