utterances.text: And I've heard this anecdotally from people on the street and who are working in EMS and everything else.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So, again, I'm going to reiterate what the speaker said, what the chair said, what all of my colleagues are going to say about that we have to get the pay up for EMTs and paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So that's one.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The other, so I have some questions as well.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: One is, when you talk about response time, is that still point to point, like when they get to the address or they get upstairs?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So response time is calculated from when the call is made to 911 until we get on the scene of the assignment.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: On the scene, so that's in the street.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I just want to point out to everybody that there's more, the response time is higher because you've got to get up to the patient.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So that doesn't include getting up to the patient.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I just, I want to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So that extends it.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: That's number one.

chapters.summary: Schulman asks how many EMS calls are routed to FDNY fire companies and whether FDNY is planning for new housing and population growth. Esposito says fire companies routinely handle about 1,000 CFR medical runs per day and that FDNY is looking at technology and AI to guide resource placement.
chapters.title: Shulman asks about FDNY CFR medical runs and housing growth planning

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The other is that I want to ask you, I'm very close to the firehouse.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: By the way, EMS and fire does a spectacular job, and I actually participated in Community Day this past weekend.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: But the firefighters are telling me that they're responding.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: In fact, when I was sitting there, they had to respond to an EMS call.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So my question is, how many EMS calls are routed to FDNY during any particular tour?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Our fire companies routinely are doing about 1,000 CFR medical emergency runs each 24-hour period each day.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So some companies might be doing 10 or 12, while other companies might only have one or two.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Does that depend what's in the queue?

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Like if there's a backlog, they'll go out?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They do not go out on the backlog.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It's simply if it's a segment one, two, or three, and then if that engine is available.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: The other thing, too, is that I want to mention, you know, the city is in a position now where we're building a lot of affordable housing and doing a lot of construction and everything else.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So you're going to have a lot more people living in different places.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And so I presume that the system will be inundated with more.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: With more 911 calls because you're going to have more people living in all different parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Are you planning for that separate from the problems that exist now?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As I had mentioned earlier in my testimony about trying to use technology and AI to best tell us where we should move and put resources.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It is something that we are looking at.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And I'm also going to say whatever you, and by the way, I've given funding for equipment for Aphidney.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: I've given money for equipment for EMS.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: So I just, you know, we're big supporters here.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: You've got to let us know what you need so we can push in the speaker, and everybody is behind this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: And like I said, I appreciate everything that you do, and let's figure out how to resolve this.

utterances.speaker: Lynn C. Schulman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we do thank the council for, we know that you've supported us with driving simulators and conditions vehicles and response vehicles.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Now, Councilmember Brooks-Powers.

chapters.summary: Council Member Selvena Brooks-Powers says response time stops when the ambulance arrives, but for isolated communities the clock runs until hospital arrival. She asks FDNY for full 911-to-hospital time by council district and why Queens saw a drop in calls reached within 10 minutes; Miano says he will look for the data.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks for end-to-end time to hospital by district

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs, and thank you to the agencies represented today.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: At last month's hearing on the Rockaways, FDNY testified that EMS response times on the peninsula are below the citywide average, but response time stops the moment the ambulance arrives, as it was just indicated again.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: For a resident of the Rockaways or another isolated community, the clock that matters runs until they reach a hospital that they can receive treatment.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can the FDNY provide these committees with the full time from the 911 call to the hospital arrival by council district?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Right now, I cannot, but it is something that we will look for.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: When we get back, we'll look for it and provide you what we have.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Queens saw the biggest drop of any borough this year in calls reached within 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Can you share why this is, especially with a decreased number of calls overall?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And just a follow-up right before you answer that.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Is FDNY currently monitoring how often areas are affected by not having sufficient ambulance coverage?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And does that lack of coverage contribute to delayed calls?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I'll do your last question first.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We actively monitor 24 hours a day call volume throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And our CRCC, which is our Central Coordination Resource Center, that redeploys ambulances from one area of the city to another, areas that have a

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: lower call volume and higher availability into areas that have a higher call volume and lower availability.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we are constantly monitoring that and moving units around.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: You know, the NY in FDNY truly stands for New York City.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: An ambulance that starts its day in one part of a borough may end up in another part of a borough, you know, to assist and help anywhere that we have deficiencies in coverage.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: As far as call volume goes.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We've already responded to 1.2 million calls this year, and over 480,000 of those calls have been of segment one through three or life-threatening emergency calls.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So our call volume remains high.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And if you can just...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I don't remember the whole question you asked first.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: The one right before that one was just talking about Queens as a borough, seeing a drop, the biggest drop of any borough this year in calls reached within 10 minutes, I think it was said.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: But we wanted to understand better as to why, considering that there's been a decreased number of...

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Of calls overall?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I don't think the call volume decrease has been substantial enough.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Like I said, we are at the middle of October, towards the end of October, and we've already responded to 1.2 million calls.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I think we are right on par with where we've been over the last few years.

chapters.summary: Brooks-Powers asks whether 911 callers are told how soon help should be expected. Esposito says call takers do not know ambulance status and it would take work to share dispatch information, but he agrees FDNY should work with the council on that.
chapters.title: Brooks-Powers asks whether callers are told ambulance ETA

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: And my last question is in respects to the chairs bill, 990, intro 990 and the ambulance delays.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Right now, if your ambulance is delayed or your area does not have an ambulance immediately available, no one tells you that information.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Are 911 callers told how soon they should expect help?

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: When a call is made.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: I know when I've called 911.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: been told that someone's on the way, but I don't recall ever being told necessarily the window of time.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And this is what I think we can work on, because the person answering the phone that you're speaking to doesn't know the status of the ambulances or what's available or what part might not be available.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That's on the dispatcher's part.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So we should work together to figure out how we can share that information.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So if there is not an ambulance coming soon, that they would know.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Selvena N. Brooks-Powers
utterances.text: Councilmember Epstein.

chapters.summary: Council Member Harvey Epstein asks whether ambulances are GPS-tracked and whether any of that information is public-facing. Miano says ambulances are tracked internally to dispatch the closest unit, but there is no public interface and no way for callers to get updated ETA information.
chapters.title: Epstein asks for public-facing ambulance tracking and callback info

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you for all being here.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So it sounds like there's consensus that we need to pay our EMSs more.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It sounds like there's some opportunity to be working on that in the, either this year and then through negotiations or next year in the budget.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: But I think we're trying to look at what's happening, the public-facing aspect of it, and we're trying to ensure the public has good, accurate information so they can

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: be able to make informed choices about waiting a half hour or getting into a cab or making other choices about maybe not the priority emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like what system, you know, like are there all the EMS vehicles, are they GPS tracked?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So there's the current system to monitor where those vehicles are and where they're going, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yes, and that's how we determine which, aside from acuity, whether it needs an ALS or a BLS ambulance, that's how we determine which ambulance is closest to respond to that call.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And none of that is publicly facing, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: None of that information is publicly facing.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Meaning that someone can log in and see where ambulances are.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, there's ambulances on the way.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's no way to know if that's actually true, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: No, currently no.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's no way for someone to call 911 back again to be able to say, hey, how soon is an ambulance coming?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: There's no way to do that, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you understand the concern that people have that, you know, my kid broke his leg and we're waiting at the playground for the ambulance to come.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if it's going to be an hour, I may make a different choice than sitting there for an hour with my kid who's in pain with a broken leg, right?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I think we're all trying to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I appreciate everything that you're saying, and I think we appreciate what the bill is intended to do.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But, you know, in this situation, like the speaker's constituent who called, right, we had ambulances responding.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we don't want, but a higher acuity call came in and they needed to be redirected.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we don't want to.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Tell somebody.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: You can tell them, hey, you know what?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We had an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: They were redirected.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We're letting you know this ambulance is redirected, and we're looking for another ambulance to send to you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So that, like, information, I know people...

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: We're busy, but there's maybe some automation that can help in that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's like we all have the technologies out there that we can do more publicly facing technology to help people with this information.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We agree and we will take a look at that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We know that when they have the information that it might not be coming soon, that they might take alternate action.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And that saves the system in sending an hour later a vehicle that there's no one there waiting for anymore.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks H&H about expanding the SHOW homeless outreach program, the Bridge to Home program, and B-HEARD mental health response. Motzquist says he is not familiar with some details but will follow up, and notes H&H works with 911, FDNY, and NYPD on B-HEARD.
chapters.title: Epstein asks H&H about SHOW, Bridge to Home, and B-HEARD expansion

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I want to just turn to the H&H for all possible.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I'm wondering, so we have the show program, which sends people out from H&H systems to locations.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering, has there been a conversation about expanding show to relieve some of the tension on some of these calls?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I apologize, I'm not familiar with the show program.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: It's basically the homeless outreach and wellness program.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then we have show vans down by me that come from Bellevue and up in Harlem.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So it would be great to know from H&H where you guys are thinking about show and the expansion of show.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, I would have to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I really appreciate you getting back to me about that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And how about Bridge to Home?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Like, you know, do you know about the Bridge to Home program?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I'm not as familiar with that as well.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay, so the Bridge to Home program, which is another program operated at H&H, which I think you should become familiar with because this is NHH.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: program creates beds inside of hospitals that provide ongoing care for people where they have a door and allows people who may be in and out of the system to have a stable place

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: to be till they can get into a supportive housing unit.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So I'm wondering from H&A's perspective, what's the opportunities to expand on Bridge to Home, which may also reduce some of the call volumes we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, I will get back to you on that information.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, I'd appreciate that too.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And then I know we talk a lot about Be Heard and kind of the pathway to Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I'm wondering how H&A is operationalizing the expansion of Be Heard.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Once again, those are great details I don't have ready for you right now.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I can get back to you on it, but I know we are partnering with 911, FDNY, and MPD to expand that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Yeah, it'd be great to know more details about what that would look like and what that expansion looks like, because I think we're trying to put relief valves on the system.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And if we can't, you know, in short term, we need to figure out what that is.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And some of these programs can really be those relief valves to take the pressure off the 911 system for people who have emergency needs, but maybe don't need to call an ambulance if there are other tools like the show van, which is out in the neighborhood already,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: or other programs that might be available to help people who have acute needs get some support that they need.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, I do want to redirect back to the virtual express care, which we talked about earlier, about how we help with DMY by answering calls for them and providing care on the spot and also preventing an ambulance from being dispatched to that call originally.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Council Member Brewer and then Pierina Sanchez.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer asks about calls that are not true emergencies and how to educate the public on alternatives. Miano says people often believe arriving by ambulance gets them seen faster, but triage is based on condition, and FDNY uses telehealth and education to divert appropriate calls.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about non-emergency 911 calls and public education

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One is, I know you have addressed already a little bit, I don't know what you call them, calls that are not emergencies, but people...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Literally, you're sometimes just calling an ambulance to get to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So how you heard earlier some suggestions maybe how to address that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: People don't read.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They don't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's not easy to address.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But is it about what's the percentage of...

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Calls that maybe could be handled elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think you have a pretty high number for that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm just trying to think of how we can work on that together, because I know people that do they call the ambulance when really they don't need it.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that there is, as stated earlier, there is a misconception of if I arrive by ambulance, I will be seen at the hospital sooner.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: However, you know, as we've as we've spoken.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Multiple times today, there is a triage process.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So it's not how you got there, it's why you're there, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And, but I think the main thing is that someone who calls 911, I would believe thinks they are having an emergency.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I don't know if we want to discourage people from calling 911, but as stated, better educate on what an emergency, what are the signs of a heart attack?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: What are the signs of someone having

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: an anaphylactic reaction, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think if we educate and start young, start early and educating on what an emergency looks like, it will help us later on.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I also think that, you know, we do have some other things in place like discussed, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We do have some telehealth stuff where we can, you know, transfer calls to a physician and speak to the physician, you know, without sending an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But I think that that is new.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Relatively new and it's generational.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think that when people right now want medical care, they want to see someone in front of them, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think that as that becomes more normalized, it'll also assist us in being able to divert some of those calls to 911 to that type of care.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, I think we'd love to work with you on the education of that in our newsletters, in our forums, et cetera, because I know people who I think abuse the system.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about ambulance and fire support in Hudson Yards and complains about siren noise from hospitals. Esposito says FDNY previously placed a rapid response vehicle in Hudson Yards and will review response times, and says sirens are required when going through intersections against traffic signals.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about Hudson Yards ambulance support and siren noise

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, I, too, go to the open firehouses, and we've allocated funding for some of them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They want a firehouse and ambulance support in Hudson Yards.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Have you heard any discussion about this at all, Hudson Yards?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Or not?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, maybe it's more on the fire than the ambulance, but it's a feeling of not enough support there.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We did look at that when they opened Hudson Yards, and when they first opened, we did put a rapid response vehicle staffed in there.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And at the time, and that's obviously going back a bunch of years, the call volume didn't seem to warrant it.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But we'll take a look at the response times over there and see what the need is on both the fire and medical.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The other question, which is not, how do the sirens play a role?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I am swamped with people who hate the sirens.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Swamped.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so I know you're trying to get through traffic, et cetera, but between the rumbler, the siren, et cetera, do you have some, we have bills on this topic.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I live between two hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My community lives between two hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's a constant complaint.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Three o'clock in the morning, I don't know what kind of traffic you're going through.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So is that something that comes up?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is there a reason to keep the sirens?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is it help with response time?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We are required, especially as you go through intersections against a red light or a stop sign, we're required when there's traffic to use the sirens to make sure everybody is alerted to that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, but there are different kinds of sirens.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have on our ambulances, our ambulances acknowledge or are in accordance with the decibel maximum.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But we don't run the only ambulances in the city.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm just talking about your ambulances because I know that's what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But it's, you know, it is loud.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They are all equipped with the rumblers so that you can, you know, feel that even at times when you don't hear it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I want you to know that the 311 calls are not able to be taken about sirens.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We're trying to change that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But in addition, I can say that it's a big quality of life issue.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks for the elevator pitch on what needs to be addressed, citing pay, lack of ambulances, and traffic. Esposito says staffing is the overwhelming issue and that EMS must become a career, which depends on fixing pay.
chapters.title: Brewer asks for the single biggest EMS problem; Esposito says staffing

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then just finally, I think my question is just generally, what is it that you, I mean, is it?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All combination of the challenges.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's the pay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's the lack of ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I assume it's traffic also.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What is the combination just in sort of like the elevator pitch as to what needs to be addressed on this?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Because it is really making people in the communities frightened and scared.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It is the staffing issue is, in my opinion, the overwhelming, the biggest issue.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have to make sure to make EMS a career, right?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That people go there for a career, not that just go in there until they're waiting to do something else, waiting to go to fire, waiting to go to sanitation, waiting to get another job.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we believe, and the commissioner strongly believes, that if we address the pay issue, we will have people that come here for a career and stay.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And, you know, there's a big difference between getting somebody that has taken a training class and has a little bit of experience to somebody that's been doing this for 10 or 12 or 15 years, right?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They are very experienced paramedic or EMT.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Just by looking at you and getting you to say a couple of words, has a very good chance of properly diagnosing you.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And that takes years of experience to get that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And that is what our goal is.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We all agree with that one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Council Member Pierina Ana Sanchez recounts a 90-year-old neighbor who fell and was cared for by NYPD for 25 minutes before an ambulance arrived. She asks how often NYPD arrives before EMS and how often police transport patients; Esposito says FDNY does not record that but knows it happens anecdotally.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks how often NYPD responds before EMS

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: First and foremost, thank you for everything that you do, for the work that your members do.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So I want to start with two experiences from my community.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Two weeks ago, my 90-year-old neighbor fell and struck his head.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: NYPD officers arrived on the scene, I want to say, within five minutes, applied pressure to his wound, cared for him for those 25 minutes remaining that it took for an ambulance to arrive.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then officers in my local precincts, the 46th, the 50th, the 52nd, they tell me how frequently patrol cars are being pulled away from other duties to respond to even nonviolent medical emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then, of course, I think everyone saw in the news when ICE shot a New Yorker in my community a little over a week ago, it was an NYPD officer who transported that father to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I do want to say I consider that officer a hero, but I think the question here is that while a life

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: saved is a life saved, these experiences are not what New Yorkers should be seeing across the city with NYPD responding to medical emergencies instead of trained professionals.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So my questions are how frequently is NYPD arriving before EMS at a medical emergency?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is it always a 100% overlap that NYPD is responding to?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: these emergencies nowadays, given the shortages, how often are police officers transporting patients to hospitals because an ambulance isn't available?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And if you don't know that, then period.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How often is NYPD transporting folks to a hospital?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I'll stop there.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So we don't record when the PD arrives before us.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: In my experience, that most of the time, the great majority of the time, either a fire engine or the ambulance arrives at the scene first.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: There are times, obviously, that the police department will be there, such as that shooting.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We had units responding.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That was obviously a shooting.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It's a priority for us, and we got there pretty quick.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The patient was already gone.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So we know anecdotally that there are times when the NYPD transports patients because we didn't have hands on the patient.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We don't have, we don't see that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We don't have a report of that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: You have numbers.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We know that with talking with the police department, they record that in their reports, and they were not able to pull it quick enough for us, for this hearing, to get it from us.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But we do know that it happens.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And let the record reflect that the chair, thank you, Madam Chair, and I did request this information yesterday morning, understanding that's not a whole lot of time, but we really do want to make sure we have that information to have a complete picture.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And then the...

chapters.summary: Sanchez asks about the training NYPD officers have when responding to medical emergencies and how EMS workers feel about police filling in. Esposito says FDNY does not know what training NYPD has, while Miano says NYPD complements EMS and that the agencies train together.
chapters.title: Sanchez asks about NYPD medical training and EMS morale

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Second question, I probably won't have time for more, but just in terms of the quality of care that happens.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: So if a police officers, we know they have basic emergency medical training, but they're not trained and equipped in the same level as EMTs and paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And that is part of the issue, right?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We don't know what training they have or what care is being given.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And I'll pass it to Chief Miano.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I do want to say that NYPD does routinely respond to EMS calls.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And it is sometimes based on...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Why we're being called, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: If there is a fight or if it's due to a motor vehicle accident, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: These are things that NYPD has to respond to.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They don't respond in place of us, but we are one emergency response service, whether it's fire, EMS, NPD, and we respond together.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And oftentimes NYPD is responding more for us, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: To make sure that we're okay, to make sure that our members are safe while operating in an environment.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chief.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And thank you, Google, also told me as much.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But a 90-year-old man, senior, you know, who falls down two steps, hits his head, there is no threat to EMS there.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so, you know, as a layperson, I'm understanding that NYPD is responding because they know that EMS will be delayed.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And so I think there's a very big question there to be answered, please.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: You know, NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And yourselves, please follow up with us.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: What is the training that they have?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And what is the training that they don't?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And I just want to be respectful of time.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: I can send these in writing and continue the conversations with you all because my questions here are founded in a deep respect, appreciation, and even love for what our EMS are doing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: And, you know, I think everybody's repeating that we need to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: But I guess I'll just close with how does this make EMS workers themselves feel?

utterances.speaker: Pierina Ana Sanchez
utterances.text: How do paramedics feel knowing that NYPD does not have the training that they do, that others do not have the training that they do, but they are nonetheless being dispatched while EMS workers are so undervalued in our city?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I know that our EMTs and paramedics, I believe, are the best trained and best experienced that we have in this country.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They get out there and they do their jobs and they are very, very good at it.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I think that competitive.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That competitive spirit and that can-do spirit that we all have in the fire department is you want to be the one that goes there and does your job.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: You don't want anybody else doing your job.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: You want to get there and provide that help and save that life.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And that's, I think, what makes our people as good as they are.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't believe that we believe that PD is responding in place of us.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I believe that we all feel that we complement each other, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Where if someone who has basic training, whether it's CFR or NYPD, can start care prior to our arrival, that's just an additional link in the chain of survival that the city is able to provide.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And that's why we do drills and we do joint training with NYPD, with the fire department, with EMS.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: That's why we work together, because when the city is in crisis, those three agencies, well, two agencies, are the ones that are stepping up.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And we need to be able to work in harmony with each other and understand everyone's limitations and also what we bring to the table.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks when the EMS CAD dispatch is created and whether it is done with NYPD, and why an unknown condition is treated as low priority. Werner says the incident enters through NYPD first, and Miano says a computer-aided triage system determines call type; unknown is the highest of the low-acuity types.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about EMS CAD dispatch and unknown-condition priority

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chiefs.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And it will be clarification for me with Council Member Sanchez's question.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So when is the EMS CAD dispatch law created?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And is that done in conjunction with the MYPD?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Is that when you're communicating with another agency?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: It's done as soon as the incident enters the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: That starts with PD.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, which would be maybe why the NYPD has access to that, right?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Right, they get the information first.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so I just want to now go back to the unknown because I think that Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Daly deserves a few more answers for her son.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So why is an unknown condition a low priority?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And why wouldn't it be considered a high priority?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Because they have not been triaged, so they don't know what the illness could be, and it could be a cardiac arrest.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we have a computer-aided triage system, right, which as callers

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: give information to questions that are asked, we enter that information into the system, and Chief Werner can expand on this, but that's what determines the call type.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It is not the individual dispatcher making a decision.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It is a computer-aided dispatch triage system that information received is placed into it, and it leads you down the road to be able to determine what the call type is.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: If we don't have the information, we don't have that to enter in in order to be able to classify it differently.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: The unknown condition is a priority for, so I'd like just to add that that is the highest priority of the low acuity types.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Of the low acuity.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But in Kevin Daly's condition, it was a high acuity.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And our dispatchers are also EMTs.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So that also comes into the low staffing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Because if you're low-staffed in general, then we're going to be low-staffed with our dispatchers as well.

chapters.summary: Ariola notes FDNY has about 4,500 budgeted EMS personnel but fewer than 4,100 on staff. Esposito says recruitment is challenging nationwide, FDNY has 163 EMT trainees at Fort Totten and about 150 in paramedic classes, and it continues testing and recruitment.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about EMS headcount and recruitment efforts

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You have 4,500 personnel, would you say?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You said earlier, was it, or in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: The budgeted amount is 4,500.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We're below 4,100, 464 spots below budgeted headcount is our actual staffing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I know that you're taking steps to increase that headcount.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Could you explain what you're doing?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So we are trying to recruit recruitment in EMS across the country since COVID-19 has been challenging.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We continue to do classes.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have 163 EMT trainees currently at our EMS Academy at Fort Totten.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And we have another 150 or so in our paramedic classes out there as well.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And so even though they're included in that head count, then that's, you know.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Below that we actually have out in the field and train in any M.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: and in the field working.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So continuing to have tests and recruit and try to fill our classes.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So if 4,500 is your optimum and 4,100 is what you have now, do you think that even if you are at 4,500, that that would be enough EMTs and paramedics to

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: be in ambulances to service a city of over a million and a half people?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That would be a great start, and that would be a good problem to have and a question to answer at that time.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks step by step what happens when no EMS call taker is available. Werner says NYPD releases the call to an EMS overflow position with a code, and the call taker enters the incident based on that code; if no call taker is available, it still goes to overflow.
chapters.title: Werner walks through overflow call handling when no call taker is available

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so I want to go back to you, Chief Werner.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Step by step, what happens when no EMS caller is available and a call comes in and it's taken?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: PD will release the call to our overflow position, which we refer to as relay.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: It will come with a code.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: And there's a call taker seated there that manages that work.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: And they will put the job into the system, the incident into the system based on the code.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, and if the call taker is unavailable?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: At the time that this incident occurred?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: At any time, if a call taker is not available.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Any time there is not a call taker available, correct.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: It goes to the overflow position.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It goes to the overflow, and then it goes to low acuity, right, number five.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Or highest of low acuity.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: It could be higher.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: No, it could be a higher acuity.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: It depends on PD interviews the caller first.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: They get the address, the borough, and they ask what's the emergency.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: And that information is transcribed into what they categorize their code as.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Some of them are pretty broad.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: There could be multiple things occurring that it would take that type of code.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: They need that code to enter the system.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: They need that code to enter it to us.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: And then we take that code and we have a list of what each code represents.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: And that's how we acquire the unknown call type.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And how long does it usually take for an unknown to get properly categorized?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: As soon as it hits their terminal, they can have it categorized within 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: It's not...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right, but we may not have...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: have an ambulance to respond.

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Well, once we entered into the system from the call-taking perspective, then it gets sent immediately to a dispatcher.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Right.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks about the pilot program placing EMTs at hospitals to speed handoffs. Miano says the hospital liaison unit was ceased at the end of May after showing only a small reduction in hospital turnaround time, and those members were returned to ambulances.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about hospital liaison unit pilot ending

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We spoke earlier, Chair Narcisse was talking about once the ambulance gets to the hospital, and I know that there was a pilot program for

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: EMTs to be at the hospital, so this way the ambulance didn't have to remain, they could hand off to a medical professional.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I don't know if that...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That pilot program is still in existence and has it been replaced by something?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we ceased that pilot program back at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: That was called the hospital liaison unit, and what that did was it had an officer and an EMT in 13 hospitals throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And when a low-acuity call was transported to the hospital, if they met that criteria of being low-acuity, then they would take over the patient's

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: care report and provide triage to the nurse, allowing that ambulance to return back to service.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: While we did see a small decrease in hospital turnaround time, the greater impact on the system was not seen.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And we felt that it would be more valuable to reduce response times by having those members back on ambulances to respond to calls.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we did cease that program.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: However, in times of...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: mass casualty incidents or large volumes of patients being transported to a hospital, we will activate an officer to respond to the hospital as a liaison to be able to better assist through that triage process with the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And since you are in contact with the hospitals, have you had productive conversation with them regarding handoff,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: EMTs getting back on the street, whether or not they would not accept a patient for a certain mental illness?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And have you had conversations with the hospitals within the H&H system?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yeah, and it's not just specific to H&H.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It's with all hospitals, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We have borough commanders, and within the boroughs we have divisions.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Those chiefs routinely with the designated Office of Medical Affairs physician that oversees that borough or that division routinely meets with hospitals to discuss

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: statistics, metrics, and work on improving, setting goals and improving on any areas that we can.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether Kevin Daly's call was ever categorized as high priority; Miano says it remained unknown and FDNY is working with NYPD to close communication gaps. Ariola also asks about the Comptroller's report on ambulance tours, and Miano says the two numbers compared are physical ambulances versus daily tours.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about Kevin Daly review and Comptroller ambulance tour report

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I know you looked, took a deep dive into Kevin Daly's particular situation.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Was it ever categorized as a high priority?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: No, it remained an unknown.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think that as we did that deep dive through, Chief Werner and her team

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: identified some areas that we can strengthen our communications with NYPD, and she is currently working with NYPD productively to be able to close those gaps.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I just want to ask, just talk about the Comptroller's report, and then I'm going to yield to you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So the Comptroller, as we know, came out with a report, and he said in spring of 2026, FDNY shifted its target number of ambulance tours per day from 488 to 332, which is a 32% reduction.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Why did it happen?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Where were tours removed?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And will this impact response times and quality of patient care?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So those two numbers are actually two separate numbers that are incorrectly being compared.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The larger number, the over 400 number, is our physical ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: That's the amount of vehicles that we actually have, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And then our tours and our units are the ones that are in service that are operating.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we have a tour count.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And our total count that we want to meet every single day is 640.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But we don't run all 640 at one time.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We run in 12-hour periods.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We run 328 during the day, and then on the evening period, we run 312.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So when those two numbers are looked at, there's an excess of ambulances, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We have 400, and then we have the 300 number.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And those extra ambulances are the ambulances that we have that are the physical vehicles that are spread throughout the city at stations.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: In case we have a mechanical issue, we're able to...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Move the unit into one of those spare vehicles.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether engine companies can refuse medical attention for patients and whether people should call volunteer or private ambulances. Esposito says only EMTs and paramedics can perform an RMA, and Miano says callers can call community volunteers directly, but 911 dispatches the closest appropriate ambulance.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about engine RMA, ambulance choice, and volunteers

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I have a question.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can an engine RMA a patient to clear the ambulances, which is refuse medical attention?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can you do that for those that don't understand?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So RMA refuses medical care when somebody calls an ambulance and then that patient, we arrive and that patient does not want to be treated.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That's a procedure we call an RMA.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Currently, only emergency medical technicians and paramedics can do that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So the firefighters on the CFR engine cannot do that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I think for safety, you don't want to IMA someone and then the person need emergency and they not access properly.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's what my assumption is.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Under our normal general guidelines, the firefighters that are certified first responders are not tasked with that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Should everyone be calling their ambulance of choice?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can they do that?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Should they be calling the private or the volunteer or the volunteer hospital?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What's your...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: If they're, I'm sorry, so volunteer agencies do have ambulances in their communities, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And that's the first and foremost, that's their job is to staff their ambulance within their community.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And if someone wants to call their community volunteers directly, they absolutely, you know, can do that.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: When you call 911, you get the closest ambulance in the 911 system to where the location is for the illness or injury.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We don't determine whether it's a municipal or a voluntary hospital ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: When we dispatch, we dispatch the closest appropriate ambulance to the location where the injured or ill person is.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I was trying to see if we can decrease the amount.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can you decrease the amount of folks running, you know, in one space and you kind of like, you know,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: moment for you, you don't have enough, and then if those volunteer ambulances, like I have Flatland,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: we have Hadzola, so would you encourage that to happen in a case that, let's say you have a question, it's not really emergency, emergency, or even for emergency.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think, again, if someone has, they're volunteers, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I don't know if we can guarantee that a volunteer is always going to be in service.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But we can guarantee that if you call 911, we have ambulances in service.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Clear.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You've made it clear.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Crystal clear.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what incentives beyond pay could help retain EMS workers. Miano says members deserve respect and acknowledgment, and the city can support quality-of-life efforts like providing Thanksgiving meals to EMS stations.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks what non-pay incentives can keep EMS workers

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Later on, I'm going to ask some of the actual workers, because I want to find out what kind of incentive we can create.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And you can tell me what kind of incentive we can create.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yes, we want the pay raise.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We want that, because people have to pay the bill.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We understand that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: New York City is very...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Very expensive to live in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We all know that, and we want our workers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What kind of incentive in your mind that we can create, even coming from our side, to make sure we're keeping our EMS workers in place in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I'm sorry, are we talking outside of pay?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Okay, so outside of pay, which I think pay is first and foremost, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But outside of pay, I think the members who are sitting behind me and the members who are on ambulances right now, I think that they deserve respect.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They deserve to be acknowledged.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They deserve to...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: be understood that when everybody else is calling for us because they need us, we're the ones that are coming.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: No matter who it is, no matter where it is, no matter the circumstances, no matter the challenge to our own safety, the members that wear the EMT and the paramedic patch in the city of New York,

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: are truly the most selfless people that you'll ever meet.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think that it's time that they get the same acknowledgement that every other emergency agency gets as well.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I'm going to say that we have the holiday season coming up.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And last year, for the first time, with the work of the unions, along with former council member Brennan,

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Thanksgiving dinners were provided to every single EMS station throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I can't tell you how much of an impact that had on the membership's morale to be able to actually have turkey on Thanksgiving instead of fast food.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We don't get the opportunity to sit inside the EMS station and have a dinner.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But to be able to grab a holiday-appropriate meal and eat it while on your lap while driving as fast as you can to somebody's emergency,

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Just knowing that somebody thought about them was tremendous.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I would just ask council if we can duplicate that again this year.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: If someone can help work with our unions and work with us.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: and provide our members with those small, little quality of life changes that make them feel as important as everyone else.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says she and the speaker will work to provide holiday meals to EMS stations and thanks Miano for the idea. Miano invites council members to visit EMS Station 58 and says broader citywide acknowledgment would help morale.
chapters.title: Narcisse commits to holiday meals and Miano invites council visits

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So appreciative of that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I mean, you can consider it done because I know Speaker Menon and my colleagues at YOLA, we're going to make sure we make it happen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And even if we have, I'm going to commit her money too.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Even if we have to do it out of our pocket, we're going to have to do it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So, yes, that's a little because I want more.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I have to acknowledge my colleague, the La Rosa, that's with us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So that's little.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But anything else you can imagine that you think that we can do beside that, because I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm ready.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You can count on me in because I love to feed people.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I love to take care of people, you know, coming from the nurse.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I'm in.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: There's a commitment.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Probably your pocket, your private money, or the city.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I don't know which way we're going to go.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: To make sure we make sure we feed all that.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I didn't mean turkey.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It was filet mignon and lobster.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm going to do everything that we can do.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because that's the least we can do.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because you're the best, guys.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I have to say that, you know, just hearing.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The passion from the council and seeing how much that the service matters, it means a lot, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I'm more than willing, along with the chief of department, the chief of emergency medical dispatch, to sit up here and answer your hard questions because we're trying to solve a problem that's going to make the emergency medical service better.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I know all of you, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Station 58 is on East 83rd and Flatlands, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We would welcome you with open arms anytime.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Just come by.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Come by.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Say hello.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They don't know I'm telling you this, but they'll be prepared for you.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think that's what we need.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I think we need more acknowledgement.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I think we need more thanks.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: This committee does that, but I think it needs to be done on a broader level citywide.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You can, we are committed.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I committed her without her knowledge already.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's how I know that she's not going to say no to that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: This is a lease that we can do.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about the hospital liaison officer program from the 2024 hearing and its results. Miano says FDNY expanded to 13 hospitals, but because the impact on response times was limited, the members were reallocated to the field; conversations with hospitals about triage continue.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks for update on hospital liaison officers and handoff process

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: At the 2024 hearing, FDNY testified that it was assigning hospital liaison officers, which is HLOS, along with two EMS.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: To nine of the busiest New York City health and hospital emergency department to facilitate patients hand off and reduce ambulance turnaround times.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can you provide an update on the implementation and results of the initiative?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Has FDNY measured any changes in ambulance turnaround times?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: availability, response times, or other operational metrics.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Which hospitals currently participate and are there plans to expand?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: modify or make the programs permanent?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I know you start talking about it earlier, but just give me more detail.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we did start initially with that amount of hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We did expand out to 13.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But like I said, while it did have a small impact on the reduction of time inside the hospital, the overall greater impact on response time was not seen.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we reallocated those members back to the field because we felt like the greatest way to impact response time was to have more ambulances available on the street.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you over is because I want to know what can we do right now?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You used the pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You repeated it for me.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Now what can we do to actually decrease it in the emergency room with the staff in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You have seen the program.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You did the pilot.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It did not work.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But I believe that you have learned from it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And what can we do?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that, you know, what's really important is the continued communication between, like I said, the borough, the division and the and the Office of Medical Affairs with the individual hospitals to work on tweaking triage systems to be able to expedite

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: patients, you know, off of stretchers and off of our stretchers and onto and onto hospital stretchers.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But each individual hospital is dynamic.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So each one has to be individually, you know, studied, spoken about, and then different things have to be implemented in each hospital.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So have you started the conversation knowing that the pilot program did not work, but we got to do something to decrease the amount of time that they spend at the triage?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So have you heard any positive feedback or whatever the feedback that you had received?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yeah, again, these conversations are happening, you know, monthly, in some locations quarterly, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They are happening and ongoing.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The increase in time after the HLU was ceased, we only saw an increase of about two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we are, you know, and this is citywide, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: This is citywide.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But I'm focused on H&H.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Right, right.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we have a great partnership with H&H.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And like I said, we are continuously working together to improve.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can you walk us through the patient handoff process from start to finish once an EMS crew arrives at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What responsibilities does the hospital liaison officer...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Oh, now you don't have that, so we're going to have to work back there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So you already gave me that part.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Since we don't have that, I will not be able.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But there's no plan to return with that because it's only two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
