utterances.text: At the moment, there is not.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how the April 2025 closures of Mount Sinai and Beth Israel affected patient volume and capacity. Motzquist says it is hard to measure causally, but Bellevue has seen a moderate increase in emergency visits and its ambulance turnaround is below the city average.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how Mount Sinai and Beth Israel closures affected H&H

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Mutsinai, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Beth, they close.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How has the closure of Mutsinai and Beth Israel in April 2025 affected patient volume?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: hospital capacity, and emergency department with times across the H&H system.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, that's really hard to measure, right?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Because you have to try to figure out where the patient originated from, where they ended up to.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We could say that overall, Bellevue has seen a moderate increase in ED visits, which may or may not be related to that closure.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It's not possible to track the exact cause of that.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: We do know that Bellevue's turnaround time with the city is below the city's average of other hospitals in getting ambulances back on the streets.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether H&H measures NYC Care's effect on avoidable emergency visits and how many New Yorkers are enrolled. Motzquist says H&H does not currently have data on that and will follow up with enrollment figures.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks H&H about NYC Care metrics and enrollment

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For some of the answers that I think we share some of the question, I thought I was getting more answers from you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But New York City care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: At a previous hearing, H&N stated that it does not collect data regarding New York City care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you know about New York City care?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Can you answer some of my questions?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I think I did before, but I can provide some more feedback if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay, I'll try to ask if you don't know it, you don't have the answer, we'll go back.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: At a previous hearing, HNA stated that it does not collect data regarding New York City Care's effect on emergency department utilization.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Has HNA since developed metrics to measure whether New York City Care is reducing avoidable emergency room visits?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: At this point, we do not, unfortunately, have the data on that.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I know that we are involved with financial counselors getting patients enrolled in New York City Care for preventive care, primary care, and virtual express care.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: But at this point in time, we don't have data to see how it's decreased emergency department visits.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many New Yorkers are currently enrolled in New York City Care, and how does that compare with enrollment levels two years ago?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: That is a great question.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: I unfortunately don't have that data for me, but I'll get it to you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So should I stop on that?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And then we can send you the questions?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because this is a fun thing, because we're supposed to...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: To talk to each other and to know exactly where we're going, how can we help?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I mean, I met people that say that when they come here this year, we ask a lot of tough questions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's not about us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's about what can we do together.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I hope that because I heard it from a DM1.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But it's not for that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's just making sure that we have to be responsible for New Yorkers and we all in it together.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We just have to get through it.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about psychiatric emergency services and the LEADS substance-use program. Motzquist says H&H treated 33,400 unique psychiatric emergency patients and 56,600 visits in 2025, and LEADS encounters rose to 30,400 with over 6,500 referrals and 3,600 naloxone kits distributed.
chapters.title: Motzquist reports psychiatric emergency and LEADS program numbers

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: H&H previously reported serving approximately 33,000 unique patients across 55,000 psychiatric emergency services and comprehensive psychiatric emergency programs.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How have those figures changed over the past two years?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So those numbers have increased slightly.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So in 2025, we treated 33,400 unique patients, of which 56,600 visits were our three psychiatric emergency services, our eight adult and child CPAP psychiatric comprehensive psychiatric emergency programs.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So it went from 33,000 to 33,400 and 55,000.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Visits for 56,600 visits.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Emergency Department Leads or ED Leads is an H&H program that places

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: licensed clinicians and peer counselors in emergency department to identify patients at risk for substance use disorders and connect them to treatment and support services at H&H.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Reported over 22,500 in the ED leads encounters in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What are the most recent numbers and what outcomes have been achieved?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: Yeah, the LEADS program is a great program.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: One of the hardest things we deal with in the emergency department is substance use.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You have a soft voice, you know that, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But I want people that are watching us and people in the back to hear.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: As I guess an emergency doctor, I don't get too excited, and I try to maintain my calm.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: The LEADS program is a great program.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It really helps get people plugged into substance abuse care.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: It's one of the hardest things we deal with in the emergency department.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: So you said in 2023, we had 22,500 encounters.

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: In 2025, that encounter rate was 30,400.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: Josh Motzquist
utterances.text: There were over 6,500 referrals to outpatient clinics and over 3,600 naloxone kits distributed.

chapters.summary: Narcisse calls Bridge to Home a great program for patients with mental illness and says she wants to keep people out of emergency rooms and off the streets. She says supportive housing and programs like SHOW should be expanded.
chapters.title: Narcisse praises Bridge to Home and mental health diversion

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: By the way, I want to talk about follow-up with my colleagues earlier about Bridge to Home.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's a great program.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And Dr.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Katz's baby and my baby, too, because the minute he called me, I was so excited.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because when you discharge a patient with a mental illness and sending them back to the street, and that's what we, a lot of people on our streets, and I'm seeing people with gowns.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm seeing people talking to themselves and just coming out of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So Bridge to Home is a baby to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Katz, and I love that baby as well.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Supportive housing and show other places that my colleagues was trying to tell you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Those are the places that we should push more so we have less folks with mental health in our train station, in different places.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We want them to be not in the emergency room.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We have freaking flyers when I used to be in the ER.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We know certain people just come because of whatever mentally going on, or maybe they need to be warm, or sometimes they need a little cool of AC.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So whatever that we can do to triage those folks, not even the triage nurse, because they are freaking fires, and they don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: By the time we come and assess them, we can see that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We can ask them the question, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And sometimes they be kind of like very honest to the nurses.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We can come back and ask them, and they don't have to.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I think I want to sign up.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Chair, I think I want to hear from the EMS workers themselves.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I have two things that we're supposed to do for them.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we talked about it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But any more questions, you can continue with your questions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I'm going to take a break.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks what specific gaps are being addressed in NYPD and FDNY dispatch communications. Werner says they are improving methods for sending and receiving messages, and Ariola requests that all call transcripts related to Kevin Daly be sent to committee counsel.
chapters.title: Ariola asks about NYPD/FDNY dispatch gaps and requests Daly call transcript

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so what are the specific gaps being addressed with NYPD and FDMY dispatch communications?

utterances.speaker: Denise Werner
utterances.text: Better methods for sending and receiving messages.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask for a transcript of all the calls related to Kevin Daly.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'd like that to be sent to committee counsel.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: He'll be reaching out for that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'm going to switch gears for something that I believe.

chapters.summary: Ariola says street redesigns and closures increase response times and cites a Cortelyou Road project where the local firehouse objected. Esposito says FDNY submitted the firehouse's feedback to DOT but does not have veto power; Ariola says Local Law 6 requires that input and she will follow up.
chapters.title: Ariola raises street closures and Local Law 6 with FDNY

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Causes response times to go up and that are that street closures.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Ambulance companies and fire companies are reporting instances where emergency responses are impacted by street closures.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We've had discussions about specific streets, specific stations where complaints have been received.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: However, there's currently a street redesign

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: on Cortellu Road in Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The administration has stated that the local firehouse, which the DOT is required to get input from on that project, had many objections to the project that would affect the emergency response and public safety and their response times.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Our office alerted you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: But DOT is moving along with the project as originally presented.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: When was the last time you brought these objections to DOT's attention?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And have you asked why they're continuing to move forward with this particular project, even though the safety of the people in the area would be at risk?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So in accordance with city regulation, the local law six, we did reach out to the local fire company.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We did get their feedback and comments.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: That was provided to Department of Transportation.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: They are aware of our concerns, but as you know, we don't have veto power on that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You do through Local Law 6.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It has to be approved by the local firehouse.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That was a bill I passed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So they need input.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Input should be adhered to because the input says we will not be able to traverse this street if it is reconfigured, whether closed or bike lane or any type of

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: reconfiguration of a street.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It will impede our ability to get to a fire or any other public safety issue quickly and efficiently.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And it will impede our response times and impede our ability.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We see it all the time where...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Big rigs, big fire rigs are unable to make a turn because there's a street closure or they have to put the ladder across the street because one side of the street is closed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So that's what Local 06 was all about.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So this was a specific issue where the input from the firehouse at Cortillia Street said we cannot do our job as effectively.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: If this street configuration is changed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So local laws is still in effect.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: It's not, I know that it's, the mayor's looking to

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: First that with a referendum, but as of right now, the FDMY can push back with DOT.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We make our concerns known.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We share that information from the firehouse with DOT and DOT proceeds.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Have you spoken to the local council person in that area?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Perhaps I'll have that conversation.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about the 2024 commitment to educate New Yorkers on urgent care and non-emergency options through PSAs. Esposito says FDNY has not instituted that yet, and Narcisse says she wants to collaborate on it.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks whether FDNY expanded PSAs on when to call 911

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: At the 2024 hearing, FDNY testified that it was working to educate New Yorkers about urgent care and other non-emergency options.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: This included using PSAs on when to dial 911.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Is this being expanded?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Did it work?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Did you try it?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we've been talking and I forgot to ask that one.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have not instituted that as of yet.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But that's one of the things that, as you've been hearing about me, how we can do things better, and that's what I wanted to collaborate with.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So let's work on this.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I think that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We've had it, you know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In the permission of the chair, because she's the chair, so I still have to.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No, I'm just bothering you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We will look at that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we can work it out.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you on that one.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether FDNY tracks how many calls crews determine do not need emergency care or transport. Miano says EMS does not tell people they do not need care; if a patient wants transport, EMS provides it, and refusal is handled through an RMA.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how many 911 calls do not need ambulance transport

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: One of the things, I don't know if I forget, forgive me, I don't know if the chair had asked that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How many 911 did your crews determine on the scene did not need emergency care or an ambulance transport?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Do you track that number?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We have the number of ambulance transports.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No, my question is, I mean, on the scene,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That they don't need the emergency at this point.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So when we arrive at the scene, we don't tell someone they don't need emergency care.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: If they want to be transported to the hospital, we transport them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: If someone says, I just want to be evaluated, I just want my blood pressure taken, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And we take their blood pressure and everything seems like it's okay, and the patient decides they don't want to go to the hospital, that's where that RMA that we spoke about earlier comes into play.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But we don't go to someone's house or the location where an ambulance is called to and tell them that we're not taking them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: RMA would be very good at that point.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because if the person qualified to tell the person, whoever that they are assessing, they're good, they have the training, they're one of the best, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So taking them to the hospital, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I mean, as a registered nurse, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because if they don't need it,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's how we end up with the freaking flyers in the ER that make over, you know, overloaded the ER too.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So is that a way we can?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I think that it's some kind of, it needs more discussion, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I don't think that, but if someone calls for an ambulance, right, our job is to respond, evaluate, treat, and transport.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And if they want to be transported to the hospital, we take them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I mean, that's a tough one, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You agree?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yeah, and also, right, we can't just abandon a patient.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: There's state regulations on abandonment, and we can't just tell somebody we're not taking it and walk away.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I got that.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But, yeah, that's a tough one.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because that's why now I know why I was getting frequent fires for no reason.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because they call 911, they get in.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So, Chair, I think I've finished with my question because that's been a long process.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I don't know if you have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Oh, I just want to mention that Council Member Albadal has joined us.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And if the council members do not have any further questions, Council Member Ressler.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Sure.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lincoln Restler thanks FDNY for candor about the staffing and compensation crisis and asks about recruitment efforts and timelines. Esposito says FDNY is partnering with schools and colleges but faces a nationwide recruitment problem, and the current EMS Academy class has 163 recruits graduating in mid-December.
chapters.title: Restler asks for recruitment timeline and EMT headcount growth

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much to both of the chairs for this important hearing and greatly appreciate leadership from the department being with us today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, I have appreciated your all's, I think, candor and forthcomingness in recognizing that we have a

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: a crisis with regard to staffing and compensation of our EMTs.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I apologize that I've been in and out a little bit this morning, but just, you know, I think your testimony was clear and compelling that your response times aren't where you want them to be because we just don't have enough people power.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you speak to efforts that you're making now to increase recruitment, and what do you think a reasonable time frame is for us to expect a significant increase in our EMT headcount?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So we are partnering with the schools, colleges, trying to get the word out that we are hiring, that these are good jobs.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: But the recruitment problem going back a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Is across the country, and it's staggering us, stifling us a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I've been, I've found each of your and the commissioners,

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: kind of candor again, refreshing that kind of recognizing that if we don't increase pay, that

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: we're going to have a serious problem and we need to resolve outstanding contract issues to make sure that workers are compensated fairly to increase the, to improve recruitment and increase and improve retention.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But, you know, recognizing this has been an issue that's going on, the contract issue has been going on for some years, that there's a nationwide shortage on workers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is there any kind of plan that you can share with us today or timeline for when we think things could start to improve?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: You know, things aren't where we want them to be right now.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I, you know, recognizing collectively that there's a problem is the starting point.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But then the question is kind of what are we doing to fix it and how are we going to get there?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is there anything you can speak to of kind of how we anticipate an increase in headcount happening in the near future?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's not a resource issue.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It's just a recruitment challenge.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We continue to run our EMS Academy.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We would like to have classes of 250, and we haven't hit that goal.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you speak to the current number of people who are in classes and when they'll be graduating?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Right now we have 163 in our EMS Academy.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We started with 200.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We're down to 163, and they will graduate in the middle of December, and we'll see a pretty quick impact as they hit the field.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Do you have a timeline for the next class after that?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: It'll be early in the new year.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That a new class will begin and when will they graduate?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The recruitment period is open.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And, you know, I ask, we have a very robust recruitment unit.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Any event that you may be hosting or having where we can get room at a table, please let us know and we will bring recruitment there.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We also have a CPR training unit, which we love to bring, right, and inform people on the importance of CPR and be able to get that message out there.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So any events that you have, please contact us on recruitment, and we will make sure that we're able to get somebody out there to try and, you know, get people from your districts into our EMS Academy.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, I really– oh, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: No, I just wanted to say I really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that we want to work together to improve this.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that we've got the contract issue is the other side of this coin.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if we're improving compensation, the recruitment gets easier and the retention improves as well.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And so I really hope that the administration is able to resolve this with the unions.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I've appreciated that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: This new fire department has made clear we have some serious issues among our EMS workforce that have to be addressed, and we really are excited to start to hopefully see some progress on that very soon.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We'd love to work with you more on recruitment, and so we'll be in touch on that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's not for today's hearing, but I will just make a note for the record that I am committed to figuring out some solutions on some.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Tiren noise.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know that Councilmember Brewer's, it's a passion project for Councilmember Brewer for many years now, and we'd love to work with the department to try and improve not just the well-being of our neighbors, but the well-being of staff who deal with extraordinary noise every single day.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

chapters.summary: Narcisse shares a brief tribute to Healthy Humor, a company bringing laughter to children suffering from cancer and other illnesses in hospitals. She says she wanted to recognize the clowns who do that work and wish the children well.
chapters.title: Narcisse highlights Healthy Humor and children's hospital work

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: While you're here, I know that I work closely to do Christmas party with FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I am blessed to have the doctors to be representing H&H here and talk about, you know, all the questions.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But I promised something that I was going to do.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They never called me a clown.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Probably they did somewhere around, but not on my social media.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: They call all of us like elected official clown.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: But I have found out that there's a company, Healthy Humor, that actually for all the children that's suffering in the hospital with cancer, and I want to put this on for them to say,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: for all the clowns that are doing it,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Continue doing it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Bring laughter to those kids that are suffering in New York City and in general in our country.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And to all of the kids, God bless you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I put this to show you that, yes, I can play it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for the strength.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So we have two short follow-up questions, one from Councilmember Aldable, the other from Councilmember Brewer, and then we're going to wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Thank you for being here.

chapters.summary: Council Member Shirley Aldebol asks how long recruitment-to-hire takes and what FDNY is doing to retain EMTs and paramedics. Miano says EMS should be a career, not a stepping stone, and FDNY is working on quality-of-work-life issues while the city and unions negotiate pay.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about retention strategies and EMS career ladder

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: here with us today and thank you chair Ariel.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I have a question about retention just following up on Councilmember Ressler's question about recruitment.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You get them in the door, how long does it take for them to actually, once you recruit them, for them to get actually hired and then

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: What are you doing about retaining your workforce?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you have any ideas of how you can keep that workforce here?

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I understand that EMTs leave being an EMT to become firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: That's like the next step.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: The next progression, but there isn't anything in between.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Like there isn't within the EMT service steps or promotional steps or, or,

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: salary steps or, you know, for them to progress through, to have, to stay in a career in EMS.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: And are you thinking about that and thinking about retention strategies for this workforce?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So I...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I would push back a little bit on saying that becoming a firefighter is the next step.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: People join EMS, right, because they have a passion for the work.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think that everything that's been discussed here talks about a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: wage and that being one of the main reasons why people have to leave, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They leave for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Maybe they have other goals.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Maybe they wanted to become firefighters or they wanted to become a nurse or they wanted to become police officers.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But EMS should never be viewed as like the starting step.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: To something else, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It needs to be its own career.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We have recruitment periods.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Once those recruitment periods end, we process the members.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: They go through physicals, and then we put them right into the next class.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: It's been stated multiple times, you know, none of us sitting up here, nor the commissioner, has, you know, a role in pay, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But we fully support

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: that being a driving factor to increasing that to be able to make sure that we retain people.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But what we can do as leaders within the fire department is try and change the quality of work life that our members have.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And I think that we're taking a real hard look.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The commissioner has a long story.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The commissioner is a longstanding veteran of the emergency medical service.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: All of my staff have more than 20 years on the job.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We speak frequently with the unions, and we try and address the quality of life issues that we can address within our capabilities.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And that's just one side of what's going to make people want to stay.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Want to do the work and they enjoy coming to work, they're going to

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: to stay.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And if they're able to pay their bills, they're going to stay, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So we will work on our part about making sure that we're doing everything we can to improve their quality of work life while the unions and the city are working on the pay side.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And in the EMS, there are significant promotional opportunities.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: As you come in as an EMT, you can stay in our HAZTAC, which is some specially trained hazmat people.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: You're able to promote to paramedic.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: You can become a rescue medic, a HAZTAC and medic.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And then we promote up Chief Miano and Chief Werner, promote it up through the EMS side, up to chief of EMS.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks whether FDNY is aware of how many collective bargaining meetings EMS unions have had with the mayor's office. Esposito says he does not know the number but is told there are positive actions.
chapters.title: Ariola asks how many collective bargaining meetings have occurred

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As long as we're on that topic, though, because you mentioned the collective bargaining, so are you aware of how many

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: collective bargaining meetings that the FDNY EMS have had with the unions and the mayor's office, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I'm told that there are, you know, positive actions going on.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks what incentives besides pay FDNY offers and how it addresses mental health and wellness. Miano cites tuition reimbursement, the FDNY Foundation, the EMS Help Fund, union assistance networks, peer support, and counseling services.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about incentives and wellness supports for EMS

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: In the incentive, which I'm very much, you know, from my business background, incentive to keep them within the structure.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: You give us advice and what we need to do, like what we all can do to let the EMS knows that we love them, we appreciate them, we respect them.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How about within the structure itself?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What are the incentives that you're giving beside the paycheck to help them, to encourage them to stay within the structure?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So the department offers a wide variety of different things.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I guess we can call or consider them incentives.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Like there is tuition reimbursement for college, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: You can work here at the fire department and earn a degree.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Myself.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Myself sitting in front of you, earned my bachelor's and my master's degree through the assistance of the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So that is one way that

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I guess we can call it an incentive to know that we have that backing.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We have other agencies like, I'm sorry, not agencies, but we have the FDNY Foundation.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We have the EMS Help Fund.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: These are all, they all.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Collaborate and have programs with different type of assistance that they can provide to our members, including the unions.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: The unions have a very substantial network of people who can assist them with financial

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: mortgages, you know, attorney, just other life things.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So when you look at that, and I don't know if we want to call them incentives, but we have these things available within the department, within the unions, within

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: organizations that are interested in helping us that you only get by being a part of this department.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: About wellness, since we're dealing with a lot of stress, especially that kind of work that we do, like in the ER or EMT, to deal with clients, how are we addressing mental health, wellness, encouragement within the structure?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: So the first part of...

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Being able to address that is having someone come forward and say, I need help, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We can acknowledge that somebody may be having an issue and we can say to them, hey, we have these things available for you, like our peer support system, like our counseling service unit.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: We partner with New York City well, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: But we have to, people have to accept the help.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And we are working on breaking that stigma of being a sign of weakness to say something is bothering me.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: You know, I spoke earlier about being able to save a life and deliver a baby, but there's nothing worse than having to look at a parent while you're unable to help their child, right?

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Nothing worse than able to look at a child while you're unable to help their parent or their grandparent.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: I can't tell you throughout my 27-year career how many times on Christmas morning I've worked cardiac arrest under a Christmas tree while families are watching.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: Those are things that will weigh on you for the remainder of your life.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And it's up to you to be able to say, I need the help.

utterances.speaker: Paul Miano
utterances.text: And this department is doing, along with the collaboration with the unions, is doing everything possible to be able to get people who need help, help.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Hero care and hero need care as well.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what percentage of EMS workers come from the military, whether a 911 education app still exists, and what happened to a National Science Foundation grant on response times. Esposito says he will look into the app, veteran percentage, and grant status.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about military recruitment, 911 app, and NSF grant

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: The new head of OLR is a rock star, so she'll figure all this out.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have two questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Quickly, military.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A lot of the EMTs I know come from the military, so I'm wondering what the percentage is and then how you do recruitment there.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That's question number one.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Second is, I think at one point there was some kind of an app to tell us this is what you call 911 for.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I wish New Yorkers understood this, and this is what you call, you know, other means.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Don't use 911.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In this case, maybe use telehealth, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that app still in play?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then just finally, I think the fire department got at one point some kind of a National Science Foundation grant to help with response times at $2 million.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I was just wondering what happened to that initiative.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: So concerning the app, I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We'll look in to see if that, you know, what the status of that is.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We will get the percentage of veterans, military veterans that are in EMS.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And do you recruit from them, from the military?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: We would certainly hire, and I guess we could look at some recruitment with them as well.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the $2 million grant?

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: And I'll look into this grant from, is it National Institute of Health?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: National Institute of Health, NSF, yes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And let's talk about response time.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Esposito
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola says the hearing has produced productive discussion and that EMS workers need compensation, uniformed first responder status, civil service status, and promotional exams. She thanks the panel and dismisses them, saying the mayor inherited the problem but must now solve it.
chapters.title: Ariola closes panel portion with push for EMS pay, status, and career ladder

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, so I think we've really discussed so many very productive things here today, and I think incentivizing is very good.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I think that until they are properly paid, making them feel as though they are valued,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: and a topic of conversation, that they're not just forgotten, that they're not just out in the street.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They are the topic of the conversation here, in the press, in the administration, at the council office, at the speaker's office.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They are probably the most talked about.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Division within the FDNY right now are the EMTs.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I think we need to, in addition to the

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: compensation, we need to give them uniformed first responder status.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We need to give them civil service status.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We need to recognize EMS civil service exams for an EMT or captain, deputy chief, division chief, whatever it is, let them know that they can

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: rise up in the ranks as you did and that there is a way.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I am completely dedicated to the FDMY, EMS, and any branch of service that are public servants and protect the lives of the people

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: in this city.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That is why chairing this committee is so important to me.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That is why we ask the questions over and over again.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I cannot tell you how appreciative I am for the answers that all of you, even H&H, you know, we know you belong to all of us, but

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: your preparedness, your heart for the job, what you want is what we want, and we all know at the end of the day what we need first is more money.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For our EMTs.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And in conversations that we've had, I am with the unions and the unions will testify,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I do believe we're at a precipice right now where we have the ear of the public, the ear of government, and the unions will be able, I feel,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: very confident to strike a very good collective bargaining agreement now, even though it has been passed over for so long.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I don't think there's ever been a time where more people and more levels of government were looking at the discrepancy and the disgrace in pay equity for EMS workers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thankfulness for the job that they do.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, thank you all so very much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Your portion is over.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Please, you're dismissed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The panel is dismissed, and we will go to public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So, yeah, there will be someone from the mayor's office staying as well as someone from fire department staying through the public.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They won't be questioned, but I want them to be able to hear what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola opens the public hearing portion, reminds attendees to observe decorum, and says the witness table is reserved for testifiers. She says speakers will have two minutes and written testimony can be submitted to the sergeants at arms or by email within 72 hours.
chapters.title: Ariola opens public testimony and sets two-minute rule

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I am now opening the public hearing portion of, yes.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'm now opening the hearing for public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I remind the members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: They may submit transcripts of such recordings to the sergeants at arms for inclusion in the hearing record.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant at arms and wait to be recognized.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on today's oversight topic, hearing topic, ambulance response times.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: If you have a written statement or additional written testimony and you wish to submit that to the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the sergeants at arms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You may also email written testimony to testimony at council.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Dot nyc dot gov that's testimony at council dot

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: nyc.gov within 72 hours of the close of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Audio and video recordings will not be accepted.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For in-person panelists, please come to the table once your name has been called.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I will now call the first witnesses, Michael Greco, president of Local 2507, Vincent Varioli, EMS Officers Union, Local 3621, and Anthony LaMorena,

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Local 3621, FDNY EMS officers.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much for coming to testify in person today.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: You can pick who goes first.

chapters.summary: Michael Greco, president of Local 2507, says he is angry and frustrated because New Yorkers are waiting too long for ambulances. He cites Comptroller data showing life-threatening ambulance response times up more than 41% since fiscal 2015 and more than 500 EMTs leaving in fiscal 2026, and recounts delayed responses including a 14-year-old stroke patient.
chapters.title: Greco testifies EMS is out of time and response times have worsened

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairperson.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I didn't know whether I should start with testimony or all that rebuttal, but we'll go with the testimony first.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Good morning, Councilmember Areola, Chairperson, and members of the New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: My name is Michael Greco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I am the president of Local 2507, representing the EMTs, paramedics, and fire inspectors who serve the people of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I am here today angry, frustrated, and deeply concerned because we are running out of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: New Yorkers are calling 911 for help, and our emergency medical system is struggling to get ambulances to them in time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We cannot continue to accept this as normal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We cannot keep holding hearings, issuing reports, and making promises while people wait for help that may not arrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The Comptroller's report confirms what our members have been warning about for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Life-threatening ambulance response times have increased more than 41% since fiscal 2015.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: More than 500 EMTs have left their position in fiscal 2026 alone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: These are not just statistics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: These are people whose lives are hanging in the balance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Recently, a 14-year-old Queens student suffered a stroke at a school.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: His school nurse called 911 and repeated calls were made, but an ambulance did not arrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: His parents ultimately drove the hospital themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: In East Harlem, a 22-year-old reportedly waited more than an hour.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: for an ambulance after an apparent overdose.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Police eventually transported him to the hospital where he was pronounced dead.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We cannot say that every delayed response results in death, but we can also not pretend that delays like these carry no consequences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: When someone is suffering a stroke,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: cardiac arrest, or a life-threatening overdose, minutes matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Every unnecessary minute is a risk we should not be asking New Yorkers to take.

chapters.summary: Greco says FDNY may be training as many EMTs as it can, but the city is losing more EMTs and paramedics than it can replace. He says the problem is retention caused by EMS being devalued, underpaid, and under-resourced, and he compares EMT and firefighter salaries after five years.
chapters.title: Greco says retention, not training, is the workforce crisis

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The FDNY tells us it's training as many EMTs as capacity allows, but that should alarm this city council, not reassure it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We are still losing more EMTs and paramedics than we can train and bring into the system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The problem is not training new recruits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: It's retaining the EMTs and paramedics we already hired.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: You cannot train your way out of a workforce crisis when you refuse to address why people are leaving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The reason for systemic delays, staffing shortages, and long wait times facing FDNY EMS is because of the way EMS is devalued, underpaid, and under-resourced in the FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: This is a result of a tale of two departments in which one of the co-equal branches of the FDNY's uniform emergency response system is not recognized as uniform and not treated equally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The only way to solve this problem is to change policies and provide pay equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: This is the obvious result of EMS not being provided uniform status, only being budgeted a quarter of the uniform staff while responding to 75% of the calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And severely underpaid is what you are seeing today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: All of the discussions about efficiency, EMS are incredibly efficient, not taking meal or bathroom breaks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Traffic?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Traffic has always existed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The difference now is that units have to travel further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: With less staff to get to emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And dispatch time, again, traveling longer is the result of being understaffed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: That misses the point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: An attempt to blame EMS for a systemic and cultural problem in the FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Compensation is a major part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: An EMT with five years experience earns approximately $60,000 in base salary compared with $109,000 for a firefighter of the same time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: That disparity makes recruitment more difficult and drives experienced professionals away.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: These are people responding to the same emergencies, entering dangerous situations, and carrying enormous responsibility for protecting human life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: How can the city expect to retain an experienced workforce while treating these professionals as though their service is worth substantially less?

chapters.summary: Greco says Local 2507's lawsuit is about whether the city recognizes EMS as essential public safety personnel. He calls fair compensation an investment in people who answer 911 calls and urges a fair contract, competitive pay, and equitable treatment.
chapters.title: Greco says Local 2507 lawsuit challenges inequitable EMS treatment

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Local 2507's lawsuit challenging the city's inequitable treatment of EMS personnel is about more than a contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: It's about whether the city recognizes EMS as an essential part of the public safety system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Fair compensation is not simply a labor benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: It's an investment in the people who answer 911 calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Our members are working class New Yorkers too.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: They are people getting up every day, putting on their uniforms, answering the call when someone is having the worst day of their life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: They deserve to be able to afford to live in the city they serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: They deserve a fair contract, competitive compensation, equitable treatment, and real commitment to retaining the experienced professionals this system desperately needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I hope that you will recognize this for what it is, one of the greatest challenges facing public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: They deserve a fair contract.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: They're experienced professionals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We are losing ground.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We are losing experienced personnel.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: New Yorkers are waiting far too long for emergency care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: But we can turn this around.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We can invest in our workforce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We can give our members a fair contract, give New Yorkers the emergency medical system they deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We are ready to work with anyone to get that done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: But the city can't wait any longer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola asks the union panel whether collective bargaining meetings have occurred with the mayor or OLR and how many. Greco says bargaining started two years ago, has stalled, and this year there have been no traditional bargaining meetings; he says conversations are positive but under confidentiality.
chapters.title: Ariola asks Greco about collective bargaining status

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So I'm going to ask each of you the same question, which was the last question that I asked of the administration.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are you...

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Are you able to state that there have been collective bargaining meetings with the mayor or his OLR staff?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And if so, how many have you had?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Our collective bargaining started two years ago, so I can't give you the number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: It's stalled.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: This particular year, we have not had a collective bargaining meeting in that traditional sense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We are currently under confidentiality to discuss the extent of the conversations we are having.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: They have been positive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: But like I've said to the new OLR commissioner, positivity and $3 get me on a subway.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So we have been left on the altar way too many times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So as positive as this is, every day we wait, another person will die.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So we look forward to continuing these conversations, and we hope to get to a resolution that's both equitable treatment to us and a fair, equitable wage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: But we are in a positive, hopeful status.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, good.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

chapters.summary: Vince Variale, president of the Uniformed EMS Officers Union Local 3621, says New York City faces a present crisis threatening lives. He cites the Mayor's Management Report and Comptroller report, and says cardiac arrest survival rates have fallen from a high of about 35% to 16%.
chapters.title: Variale testifies EMS crisis is here and survival rates have fallen

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairwoman Joanne Areola.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I'd like to concur with President Michael Greco.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: We haven't had any collective bargaining meetings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: We had conversations, positive conversations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And yes, we have been left at the altar many times, so take that for what we can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: So my name is Vince Barriale.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I am an EMS lieutenant and president of the Uniformed EMS Officers Union, Local 3621, District Council 37, representing more than 600 EMS sergeants, lieutenants, and captains in the New York City Fire Department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I am here again to report that New York City is facing a crisis, not one that is coming, but one that is here now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: One that threatens the lives of all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: This is a warning that not only comes only from EMS unions or the fire department, both of which have repeatedly advised that inadequate staffing is hindering the delivery of timely, life-saving care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The mayor's own management report released this month, and more recently, the New York City Comptroller's report released last week, confirms the seriousness of the problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: These reports identify low wages and inferior benefits as major contributors to the poor recruitment and declining retention in EMS ranks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: As a result, the city cannot consistently staff enough ambulance and officer units, response times have increased, and experienced EMS members continue to leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: What I find to be most troubling is survival rates have fallen from a high of 35% to now just a low of 16%.

chapters.summary: Variale says low wages and high response times stem from FDNY failing to treat EMS as a co-equal uniformed branch. He says EMS responds to 1.6 million calls with about 25% of staffing while fire handles about 500,000 calls with 13,000 personnel, and EMS receives about 16% of the FDNY budget.
chapters.title: Variale says FDNY treats EMS as subordinate despite medical call volume

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The problem is not just low wages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The low wages and high response times are caused by the FDA's failure to properly recognize EMS as a co-equal branch of its uniformed emergency response system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: This is a dangerous to the public and discriminates against members of EMS who are the most diverse of the first responders in the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The majority of the calls that both fire and EMS respond to are medical.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Let me say that again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: EMS and fire respond to the same emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: 85% of them are EMS calls and less than 2% are fire calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The majority of the calls that firefighters respond to are to provide medical care in non-fire medical emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: While firefighters have less training and qualifications and provide lesser skills on these calls,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: EMS responding to the same calls while providing advanced life-saving care are paid half that of firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: On top of this, EMS with 25% of the staffing are forced to handle 1.6 million calls annually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: while fire with a staffing of 13,000 handled closer to 500,000 calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Meanwhile, fire receives approximately 84% of the FDNY's budget, while EMS is given approximately 16% of the budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: This means that while we are paid half of what firefighters are paid to respond to emergencies, our fire counterparts enjoy the luxuries of firehouses, recreational facilities, state-of-the-art kitchens, and sleeping quarters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: While we in EMS are left on the street corners, forced to sit in a cab of an ambulance for 8 to 12 hours, responding back-to-back to emergencies, often without even opportunity to properly clean up or, God forbid, take a bathroom break.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Imagine the emotional and physical toll this has on members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It is easy to understand how this stark difference in treatment negatively affects the morale and has EMS leaving the job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: We can't look away from the cause of the problems we are here to discuss.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It is not about EMS efficiency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: EMS are highly efficient and somehow miraculously are able to handle 10 times the core volume of fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It is not about traffic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Traffic has always existed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The problem is when you have to send a unit from Manhattan to Staten Island to respond to an emergency due to understaffing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: That is going to slow down responses, increase response times, and we can't blame EMS or look to EMS to continue to shoulder the solution.

chapters.summary: Variale says EMS cannot be expected to shoulder the solution and that anything short of co-equal treatment is a band-aid. He asks the city to ensure EMS members are treated as equals to fire operations and to provide pay and benefits comparable to firefighters to improve recruitment and retention.
chapters.title: Variale calls for equal treatment, pay, and career retention policies

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: This problem will not go away until the city takes the steps necessary to treat EMS as a co-

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: equal branch of the FDNY's Uniformed Emergency Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Anything else is just a band-aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Every day that this crisis continues, more New Yorkers lose the chance to receive timely, life-saving care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It does not have to be this way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The mayor has the ability to negotiate a settlement that would address the conditions driving this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: EMS is among the city's most diverse uniformed emergency services, and the workforce composed predominantly of women and people of color.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The city should take the two immediate steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Ensure members of EMS are treated as equals to members of fire operations through leadership and recognition and compensation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
