utterances.text: Provide EMS personnel with the pay and benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Compatible to those of the firefighter counterparts, adopt policy changes that strengthen recruitment, improve retention, and encourage new FDNY members to build on long-term careers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Together, these actions will help stabilize the EMS workforce and improve emergency care for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Variale says EMS captain, deputy chief, and division chief became civil service titles in 2019, but the city and department refused to recognize them. He says the union won a lawsuit on eight counts, quoting the judge that the city violated EMS members' constitutional rights, yet no civil service exams have been scheduled.
chapters.title: Variale says EMS civil service promotions still not recognized

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I'd like to comment about what was last said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Regarding opportunities in EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: There are other opportunities other than going to fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: There are promotions to lieutenant, which is a civil service exam.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: There is captain, deputy chief, and division chief.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: For many years, those titles were not civil service titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They were a pick-em, basically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I like you, so I'll make you this or whatever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They did an interview, but basically if they liked the person, they would pick that person to get promoted.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: That changed in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: A law was passed and signed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: making EMS captain, deputy chief, and division chief all civil service titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The department and the city refused to recognize those, that exam, all those titles being civil service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: We filed a lawsuit, and just about a month ago, we won that lawsuit on eight counts, all in favor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I'll quote the judge on this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The city has violated the constitutional rights of the members in EMS, but not providing them with an equal and fair opportunity of merit and fitness to promote to these civil service titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And today we are still left with no civil service exam to these titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I had members, officers, lieutenants, who after hearing that this promotion is not going to be recognized still, are resigning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They took a pension loan and they're moving out to another place to get a job in another city or state that would better recognize and treat EMS better than we do in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And again, we lose more experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: That we paid for in training, that was gained through years of working with patients, and the damages continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: These are, my point is that these are not just, these things, the issues are not just about money.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: We need to make this a career, a place where people want to come and stay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Encourage those to say, hey, I want to join the EMS ranks in New York City because there is a career there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I can stay there for 20, 30 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: 30 years, earn a living, and have a ladder to go up on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Without that, the problem will continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Anthony Almojera, vice president of Local 3621, says EMS has no more time and reads daily snapshots showing 68 to 138 ambulances out of service each afternoon. He says as he spoke there were 112 ambulances off service and 51 calls holding, with many over three hours.
chapters.title: Almojera documents more than 100 ambulances out of service daily

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chairperson and members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Thank you, Chairperson Abriola, for having us, as always.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: My name is Anthony Almagera.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I am a lieutenant with FDNY EMS for 23 years and vice president of Local 3621, representing the officers of FDNY EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I will reiterate, we have been left at the altar, but I would argue we've never even been asked for our hand in marriage by the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I would like to be left at the altar to get to that point, but we've never been there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: But unfortunately, we and I would like to thank you all for your time today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: But unfortunately, we and EMS do not have any more time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And more importantly, neither do the people of New York City who call 911 expecting someone to come and save their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I want to begin by reading some numbers from this past week, which I've been documenting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: These are the numbers of ambulances out of service across New York City at 2 p.m.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Each day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Starting on October 11th, Sunday, 138 ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Monday, 89 ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Tuesday, 92 ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Wednesday, 68 ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Thursday, 94 ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Friday, 101 ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And Saturday...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: 10, 17, 122 ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Seven days, seven snapshots of a system struggling to put ambulances on the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And right now, as I'm speaking to you, I asked somebody to send me the numbers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We are 112 ambulances off service and 51 calls in holding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: The majority are over three hours, as I'm speaking to you right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: That's an average of more than 100 ambulances out of service at 2 o'clock in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: These aren't numbers on a spreadsheet to us who are working them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: These are ambulances that aren't responding to emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: These are resources that New Yorkers cannot count on when they need them.

chapters.summary: Almojera describes a Staten Island woman who waited two hours and 47 minutes, suffered heat stroke, and died, and a Long Island City woman with an open compound leg fracture who waited three hours on a hallway floor. He says these are not spreadsheets but resources New Yorkers cannot count on.
chapters.title: Almojera recounts patients who died or waited hours for ambulances

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Now let me tell you what those numbers look like when they become human beings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: In late August, on Staten Island,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: A woman suffering a medical emergency waited two hours and 47 minutes for an ambulance to arrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Two hours and 47 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: She was unable to walk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: While waiting, she suffered a heat stroke.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And she died.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: In September, a woman in Long Island City suffered an open compound fracture of her tibia and fibula, her shin bones.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: A devastating injury with broken bone exposed through the skin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: She lay on the hallway floor of her apartment building waiting for help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Not 10 minutes, not 30 minutes, three hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Three hours lying on the floor with a broken leg, waiting for an ambulance in the wealthiest city in the wealthiest country on earth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And on October 8th, during an ICE-related shooting, as the councilwoman from the Bronx mentioned, a man was shot in the neck.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: An ambulance was requested.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: But ultimately, it was NYPD officers who transported the wounded man to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Think about what that means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Immigration enforcement and ICE operations have become a major public safety concern in this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Yet when an incident involving federal immigration agents results in someone being shot, we cannot even be certain that an ambulance will be available to provide timely emergency medical care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Regardless of where anyone stands on immigration enforcement, when someone is shot, they need an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: In October, a woman in the South Bronx was suffering a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: She called 911 repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: She waited approximately two hours for an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And when an ambulance...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Finally arrived, it was too late to save her.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: She died on the way to the hospital.

chapters.summary: Almojera cites a shooting where NYPD transported the wounded man and a South Bronx heart attack patient who died after a two-hour wait. He says EMS is no longer failing but has failed, not because of EMTs and paramedics, but because dedication cannot replace staffing and ambulances.
chapters.title: Almojera says EMS has failed after decades of undervaluing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And then in the most recent incident on the Upper East Side,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: with Councilwoman Menon, thank you, publicly demanded answers from the FDNY about the ambulance that did not arrive for the patient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Think about what that means.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: A teenager is injured in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: People call 911 repeatedly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: They wait, they call again, and eventually they realize they cannot rely on an ambulance to come to help them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: This is New York City in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And I want to be absolutely clear about something today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We have spent years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: My first city council meeting was 22 years ago, saying these same things, listening to the union leaders then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We spent years warning about the direction the system was heading.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We warned about the staffing shortages, and that is what it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: There is no magic pill.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I've listened to these chiefs say, we're going to do X, Y, and Z and squeeze more blood from a stone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: There's no more blood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We warned about the pay disparity between EMS first responders and firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We warned about the loss of experienced EMTs and paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We warned about the ambulances being taken off the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We warned about the growing response times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: But we must also confront a deeper truth about how we arrived at this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: For decades, the FDNY has maintained a culture that treats EMS as a subordinate branch rather than an equal partner in public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Despite legislation enacted in 2001 recognizing the uniform status of EMS,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: New York City has continued to deny EMS the institutional recognition, respect, and resources afforded to the fireside.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Think about that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: The overwhelming majority of the emergencies firefighters respond to are in medical nature, yet the EMTs and paramedics who provide the advanced medical care wearing fire department uniforms

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: They are treated as less valuable with the very same department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: That is not merely a question of professional respect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: It is a systemic failure with consequences that extend far beyond the workforce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I am almost done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: When you systemically undervalue the people responsible for providing EMS care, you create the conditions for understaffing, attrition, longer response times, and ultimately preventable deaths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And for years, New York City has allowed this system to continue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: The patients waiting for an ambulance are now paying the price.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And for years, we have described EMS as a system that is failing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I am here to tell you today that we have passed that point.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: EMS is no longer failing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: EMS has failed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We are in failure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Not because the EMTs and paramedics have failed, not because the dispatchers have failed, not because the men and women who put on the uniform every day have stopped calling, answering the call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: They continue to show up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: They continue to work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: They continue to do everything they can with the resources they are given, but dedication cannot replace staffing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Compassion cannot replace an ambulance, and courage cannot turn a two-hour wait into a six-minute response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: The people who work EMS cannot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: keep carrying the consequences of decisions they did not take.

chapters.summary: Almojera says 47 members have reached out since 2020 saying they want to commit suicide and 14 members have died by suicide among those who reached out. He says EMS is not asking for applause but for resources and accountability when patients wait hours or die.
chapters.title: Almojera details mental health toll and demands accountability

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Councilwoman Narcisse mentioned mental health.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: 47 members have reached out to me since 2020 saying they want to commit suicide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We have had 14 members commit suicide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: That's only the people who reached out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We are not here asking for applause.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We are not asking to be called heroes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We are asking for the resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We need accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: When a patient waits three hours for an open fracture, someone needs to answer for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: When a woman waits three hours for an ambulance and dies, someone needs to answer for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Because the next person waiting for the ambulance could be your mother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Your father, your spouse, your child, as the woman who testified from your district, Councilwoman Areola.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We cannot keep calling this a crisis as though it is something that might happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: It is happening right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: People are waiting right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: People are suffering right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I began by thanking you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: I will end by reminding you that time is one thing our patients do not have, and New York City EMS has run out of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I believe Councilmember Ressler has a question for this panel.

chapters.summary: Restler asks Variale to clarify the survival rate statistic and what the decline means. Variale says the rate fell from about 35% to 16%, citing a Penn State study that experienced EMTs or paramedics with six or more years improve survival rates, and says losing veteran providers hurts outcomes.
chapters.title: Restler questions Variale on survival rate decline and experience

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Firstly, thank you all for your...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Compelling and impassioned testimony and your consistent forceful advocacy on behalf of your members it makes a real difference and we are all rooting hard for you to get these contracts done and to ensure that

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: EMTs are getting the wages that they deserve

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I just wanted to drill down, President Varielli, on a statistic that you mentioned in your testimony on survival rates, that they had fallen from 35% to 16%.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could you clarify the data points that you're referring to and from when to when have we seen this decline and what that means that the survival rate has declined so precipitously?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: So I got that from the mayor's management report that's in there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The survival rate, I believe the highest was in 2019, was 37%, between 35% and 37%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And the survival rate basically is the person, the patient was found dead, clinically dead, cardiac arrest or any other way, and then was revived by EMS and survived.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: When they were treated, transported to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: From a height of 35%, as I put on the record, that survival rate has plummeted to 16%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Now, some can say it's because the staffing isn't there, so we're not getting to the call quick enough, which is probably part of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: But a lot of it also has to do with the lack of experience because many members have gone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Members with experience have gone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And where I get that from is there is a study that was done in Penn State that showed an increase in the survival rate whenever they had an EMT or paramedic with six or more years of experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They saw an increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Of 27% on the survival rate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Now, to strengthen that study, there was a study done about 15 years ago, maybe more, in the FDNY

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: that showed whenever an EMS lieutenant was on the scene of a cardiac arrest, the survival rate of that cardiac arrest increased.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: At first you think, well, why would that be?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It's not like they have to really supervise EMTs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They know their job or paramedics or that matter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It made sense.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The majority of EMTs and paramedics have less than, I think it's 75% have less than five years experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: The majority of the officers have over seven years to 10 years experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: So again, it strengthens the research that was done by Penn State saying, if you have more than six years of experience, the survival rate will increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And that's what that meant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: So by not having enough staffing, we can't get there on time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: By not having the experience, the veterans that we need, we can't save their life.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It certainly, I really appreciate you sharing that study and that and highlighting it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: It doesn't surprise me at all that somebody with more experience on the job is better at it, right?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: As a council member, I'm better in year five.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just by what some of my colleagues might say, than I think I was in year one.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know that a teacher gets better in year five than he or she was in year one, and it really makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So ensuring that we're retaining this workforce is critically important for the health and safety and well-being of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But I still just want to drill down on this stat because it's so disturbing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Just so I make sure I understand it, forgive my ignorance.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The survival rate, it refers to the number of people that have been revived.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that right from EMT showing up?

chapters.summary: Greco says EMS responds to about 80 cardiac arrests a day, or 29,000 a year, so a drop from 37% to 16% survival means about 4,000 fewer people survive annually. Restler calls this the most compelling point of the hearing and says policymakers must solve for it.
chapters.title: Greco calculates thousands of additional cardiac arrest deaths

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So I'll put the numbers in it for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I mean, I just, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I'm the one when it comes to the numbers in my brain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I want you to elaborate further.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So we do about 80 cardiac arrests a day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So that works out to about 29,000 cardiac arrests a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: At a 16% survival rate, that means 5,000 people survived that year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: At a 37% survival rate, 9,000 people survived that year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So how do you put a cost on what is going on?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: That means 4,000 people died this year that didn't need to if they would have gone to 2019.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: That's what I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I was going to get to that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I have to say, I don't think that there is a single more compelling thing that anybody could say this entire day than that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I'm out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I really mean it.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, like how, what, for all of us as public servants, as policymakers, that is a number we have to solve for.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thousands of people that are dying in the streets of New York City that shouldn't be, that are in crisis that shouldn't be because we don't have the workforce in place that is responding in real time as well as we did just several years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The fire department's gone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Well, and that was my point when I brought the survival rate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Totally.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Because I've heard everybody talk about response times, which is very important, obviously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: We need the staffing for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: But the survival rate shows that we're losing the experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They are leaving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And I gave you that story about the two officers who left.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It's just more experience just going out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: the door because we're not doing anything to give them here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I appreciate you highlighting the importance of experienced workforce.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I think that is an important component here, but I just think the numbers themselves are profoundly different.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thousands of people are dying in New York City that shouldn't be.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Right.

chapters.summary: Almojera says FDNY is now losing officers to the fire class, taking experience out of EMS. Greco says it costs $45,000 to train an EMT and $100,000 to train a paramedic, and that the city has spent millions training people who leave for other services.
chapters.title: Union leaders add attrition and training-cost numbers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: Can I give you one more number?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: It's been brought up about this transfer to fire.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: They call it a promotion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: We are now losing officers to the fire class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: So you talk about experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: The experience strength has been traditionally the officers that has gone down over the years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And now people have moved up three ranks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anthony Almojera
utterances.text: And they're going into the fire class because they don't make enough money here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And we bring numbers since we moved to training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The chief of the department in his testimony with the promotion cycle of 358 EMTs, 63 paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Numbers help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: OLR's numbers, it costs $45,000 to train an EMT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: It costs $100,000 to train a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So that means this year we've thrown $22.3 million into training and sent them over to another service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We have done the same amount of calls this year that we have done last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The reimbursement rate this year is down $50 million, and they wanted to know why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Well, when you're holding jobs for three, four hours, and then you're making a phone call that says, hey, you still need us?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: You're not billing for that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So if for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: No other reason.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: You don't care about a life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: You don't care about nothing else.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: You just wasted $75 million on poor management.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We all know the city of New York has policies, has bureaucracies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: But if the FDNY EMS system was run as a Fortune 500 company, we would be bankrupt.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: It would be, it's terrible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Your stat of putting a human life to this is why we're having positive discussions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We've been up 22 years talking about our members homeless.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Nobody seems to care, not because they don't care about the individual, because the system won't let it done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Why are we having positive conversations?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Because in your district, in your district, in your district, people are hurting or dying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: My colleagues mentioned how we have real-time stats.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: I got a call right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: It's called a gynecological hemorrhage, which means there is a woman bleeding possibly from that area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: She's been sitting in a lobby for two hours right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: That's the stat right now as I look at the phone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So the fire department is going to come up here and say, this is a non-critical injury.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: This is New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: This is not a math problem that I need Albert Einstein to solve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Fire has a five-minute response time because they got 13,000 personnel that deal with 100,000 fires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: They are so overstaffed that they can do the overflow of 400,000 medical calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Give me 15,000 people and anybody and their mother can call 911 and get an ambulance whenever they want.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: is a crisis in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And eventually, every single one of us in this room are going to have to answer for why people are dying left and right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And that's why we're here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: As Anthony said, as Vinny said, this isn't a crisis that's coming tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: This is going on right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: If I can add to that also, the non-life-threatening calls that they hold, like as you said, two hours, and I don't consider that life-threatening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: You're bleeding out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: That's not life-threatening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: But a non-life-threatening call can very easily turn into a life-threatening call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Nobody's there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And I'm glad you brought up the unknown, the segment, the unknown they classified as a segment four.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I don't understand why it's a segment four.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It should be higher than that because it's unknown.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: How do you know it's not a cardiac arrest?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I can tell you my personal experience as an EMT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I've had a call that came over as a non-critical injury because the person said, in what I was reading on the computer, the person fell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: When I got there, the person fell because they had a heart attack.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They were in cardiac arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Now it turns into a priority one.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And now I got to ask for ambulance, for paramedics and all sorts of more resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: But if you don't know, it should be a higher priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I would think at least in the top two, three, not a four.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Because we don't know.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: And in that case, that that kid had a stroke.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I mean, I don't know how that wasn't reclassified.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I can't blame the dispatch system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: I know they're trying, working very hard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: They're also.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: Understaffed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: So, you know, all this stuff has to go back to we need to support and fund a life-saving service called EMS now to have turned this ship around because it's not going to happen overnight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: It's going to take time to do it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: So every day we wait, we're going to be waiting longer to get to see the results.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Vince Variale
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Each of your testimonies were so compelling.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And if you didn't think that we are in a state of emergency now regarding EMS and the lives that are being lost

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: daily because we don't have enough EMS and ambulances on the street because they are not compensated and cannot be retained, then I hope you know it now.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We are in a state of emergency.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Of emergency.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And I just want to end with this, that we understand this is a difficult problem to solve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And as a union, it's a pretty interesting place to be when everybody agrees with us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: So this message goes out to OLR, to the mayor's office, to the office of budget, to city council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: The union is here as the answer to your problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: We are willing to work with anybody to get this done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: And we hope we can get there before more people die.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so very much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: The next panel is Valerie Guardino, Logan Clark, and Joseph Ranieri.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Michael Greco
utterances.text: You got a date without me.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Okay, let's go.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola

chapters.summary: Logan Clark of IBO says the Mayor's Management Report shows end-to-end response times for life-threatening emergencies have increased by nearly three minutes since FY22 to more than 13 minutes. He says call volume increased 5% since 2022 but is down from its 2024 peak, while daily ambulance operating hours fell nearly 10%.
chapters.title: IBO testifies response times worsened as ambulance hours fell

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Areola, and I think that's all we've got today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: And other members of the committees on fire and emergency management and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: My name is Logan Clark, and I'm the Assistant Director of Government Operations and Community Services at the New York City Independent Budget Office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: I'm joined today by my colleague, Valerie Gudino, who is a budget and policy analyst at IBO.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: IBO is a nonpartisan government agency whose mission is to enhance understanding of New York City's budget, public policy, and economy through independent fiscal and policy analysis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: We appreciate the invitation to testify at today's hearing on ambulance response times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: IBO has analyzed emergency medical services staffing over the five years presented in the fiscal year 2026 Mayor's Management Report, or MMR.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: The recently published MMR documents longer end-to-end average response times for life-threatening medical emergencies that are designated as segment 1 to 3 incidents with

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: in the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: This system includes both FDNY ambulances and voluntary ambulances operated by the city's nonprofit hospital systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: End-to-end response time measures the total time it takes from when a caller dials 911 until an ambulance arrives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: The most recent MMR reveals that ambulance response times have increased by nearly three minutes since FY22 and now average more than 13 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: The fire department cites call volume as the primary reason contributing to this troubling increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: Although call volume has increased by 5% since 2022, it is currently down from its 2024 peak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: Even with that decline, end-to-end responses have continued to worsen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: Meanwhile, since 2022, the daily average number of ambulance operating hours in the 911 system has consistently declined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: Daily ambulance hours, including both EMS and voluntary ambulances, have decreased by nearly 10% from 8,900 in 2022 to 8,100 in 2026.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: In recent years, and as recently as January 2026, voluntary ambulance operators have made up roughly one-third of all daily ambulance tours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: However, FDNY states in the MMR that 11 hospital systems removed their ambulances from the 911 system in FY26.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: It is unclear what the exact impact of those hospitals leaving will have on the proportion of voluntary tours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: IBO does not have information on why these hospitals withdrew from the 911.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: 911 system or any staffing details for voluntary ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: IBO analyzed EMS personnel staffing levels and fluctuations from 2022 to 2026 using the city's human resource management system or charms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: EMS staffing includes emergency medical technicians who typically staff basic life support units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: EMS paramedics who staff advanced life support and paramedic response units, and EMS lieutenants and captains who supervise but typically do not go directly to calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: Out of those titles, EMTs have the lowest starting salaries but are eligible to be promoted to higher trained and paid paramedic and firefighter titles through a civil service exam.

chapters.summary: Valerie Gudino says EMS staffing has had substantial volatility from FY22 to FY26, with higher attrition among EMTs than paramedics and supervisors. She says the timing of the firefighter promotional exam creates recurring periods of high EMS attrition just as new classes are brought in.
chapters.title: Gudino details EMS staffing volatility and firefighter promotion cycle

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: There has been substantial volatility in staffing, both decreases and increases, during the period from fiscal year 2022 to fiscal year 2026, which could have affected operations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: There is higher attrition among EMTs than among paramedics and supervisors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: Many EMTs separate from the agency or look for promotional opportunities as paramedics or firefighters.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: While the number of paramedics and supervisors has remained relatively unchanged, the number of EMTs has fallen and decreased their share of the EMS workforce from 69% to 63%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: Staffing levels have also sharply increased at times as new classes are brought in roughly three times a year following a 17-week training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: With the largest month-to-month increase happening in October 2024, with 324

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: or new EMS staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: Many EMTs and paramedics take the promotional firefighter exam.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: Although providing clear access to higher paying careers is laudable, the structure and timing of the firefighter promotional exam relative to EMS hiring initiatives effectively ensures a cycle of periods of high attrition at EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: This may challenge EMS capacity, especially when coupled with standard attrition and what is already a high-stress occupation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: EMS staffing levels tend to decrease most following the establishment of a new promotional list for the firefighter title, which requires an 18-week training period, amongst other prerequisites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Valerie Gudino
utterances.text: The largest decrease, with 252 active EMS positions, occurred in March 2025, which aligns with when the 18-week training period would begin before the June firefighter class.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: There is no single cause of worsening ambulance response times, nor any simple answer to address this trend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: In the broader context of more hospitals pulling their ambulances from the 911 system, more of the call burn is being placed on FDNY EMS staff.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: This follows a nationwide trend of hospital systems dropping ambulance service, driven at least in part by insurance reimbursement rates well below the cost of providing those services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: But as one step towards a remedy, EMS can attempt to address the high levels of attrition and staff turnover and expand its capacity for more EMS classes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: The solution must consider the promotional list of firefighters and balance consistent staffing levels at EMS with providing promotional career opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Logan Clark
utterances.text: We thank you for your opportunity to testify today, and we're happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I'm glad that you did the study, and that was very smart.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Sir, please.

chapters.summary: Joseph Ranieri of the Regional EMS Council of New York City says EMS has a true retention problem and strongly opposes replacing two paramedics with one paramedic and one EMT. He says paramedics rely on each other for clinical judgment in complex cases like cardiac arrest.
chapters.title: Ranieri opposes single-paramedic staffing and urges retention focus

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilwoman Areola, and I want to thank the New York City Council for holding these public hearings and keeping EMS on the public agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: It's been far too long in the making.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So I am Joseph Ranieri.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: I'm the executive director of the Regional EMS Council of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Our body is a nonprofit organization with statutory authority under New York State public health law with coordinating EMS resources throughout our region.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: You often do not see us at these public hearings because our primary focus is in medicine, developing good medicine for our EMTs and paramedics to follow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: However, the state of our current EMS system, we felt that it is necessary for us to be here and to reinforce everything that's been stated up until this moment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: EMS has a true retention problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: One of the things I do want to specifically address was the idea about going single paramedic, having an EMT and a paramedic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: We at the council vehemently think that this is a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Paramedics treat very complex patients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: They rely on having two paramedics on the scene to bounce off of each other to help with their clinical judgment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So to give one example that Councilwoman Arcees will appreciate, in conducting a cardiac

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: arrest, the ECC guidelines recommend having a cardiac team of at least six individuals to work that arrest.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: In EMS, that often will consist of two paramedics, a supervisor, and maybe an EMT crew.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: The two paramedics are the clinicians on the scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: They are doing weight-based medications, some of which, if they get the dosing wrong, will have extremely negative effects on the patient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So I do want to specifically address that and say that having dual medics provides good medicine to our patients in the field.

chapters.summary: Ranieri says pay parity is at the top of the retention problem and EMS workers need better work-life balance, clear career paths, and incentives. He says EMS providers are people, not machines, and should not be pushed to squeeze out extra calls without recovery time.
chapters.title: Ranieri calls for pay parity, work-life balance, and recovery time

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Related to the retention issue that is at hand, obviously pay parity is at the top of the list.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: This is not something that is just occurring at the New York City level, but also at the state level and the national level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Our EMT members need better pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: They also need better work-life balance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: They need clear career paths for promotions, but also as well as incentives for them to remain in the field and treating patients at better pay and incentives, such as being a field training officer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: In addition, our EMS providers, a lot of the discussions we've heard today has been about efficiency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Efficiencies are things that we discuss on with dealing with mechanisms and machines and systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: These are people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: We should not be trying to wring an extra one or two response calls out of our EMTs and paramedics in the field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: We should be looking at what is causing them to have these high rates of call-outs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: A lot of times, unlike on the fire side, where if a firefighter responds and goes to a fire, they are given some time to recover, both physically and mentally, from that call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: However, if you've ever worked in EMS or in the hospital and you've had to work up a difficult arrest or a pediatric arrest that is both physically and emotionally demanding,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Our EMS members are often not given that same ability time to recover.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: All right, so these are all things that obviously need to be brought up with the contract negotiations that are occurring.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: One of the things I will point out, a lot of times we reference, that's been referenced throughout this hearing has been the Labor Relations Board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: I think it would be interesting to have them up here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: And speaking on these issues because it seems that the mayor is in support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Obviously, the department itself has claimed their support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: The city council, who is the will of the New York City residents, are in support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So we need to really identify where the hang-up is and what's preventing this from getting done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: I also want to address the issue with regards to that was brought up on the firefighter promotional exam.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: It is not a promotion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: It is a change in career, a change in field.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Now, it is beneficial to have firefighters that are trained in medicine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: That does help because it is an expectation of the public that when a fire company responds, that they have medical training.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Just as it is an expectation of the public that our police have some medical training, and they do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: They're trained in basic CPR and first aid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So that is a benefit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: However, particularly when we lose a paramedic to the fireside, those skills, those advanced life support skills, are not carried over to the firefighter level.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: CFR units do not carry the ALS equipment that paramedics use, and they're not exposed to the continuing medical education that's needed for a true clinician that a paramedic is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So that training, that experience is lost.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: And as has been brought up before, the less experienced providers we have, the worse outcomes there are for our patients, both in the field and then when those patients end up going back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So a lot of the efficiency things that have been brought up really are trimming around the edges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: We need to acknowledge the fact that our society relies more on medicine today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: We have more calls, more patients, more complex patients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Our EMT members that are trained today, even at the BLS level, the EMT today, right, carries twice as many medications today as they did 20 years ago when I first became an EMT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: That's medications that have to be trained on, how to administer, how to recognize the appropriate patients to give them to, the contraindications for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: We're expecting more from our providers, both in their knowledge and their skills, and how many calls they respond to, but we're not adequately compensating them the right way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So with that, I thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Narcisse thanks Ranieri and says she agrees that the city must invest in EMS at frontline and support levels. Ranieri says even online medical control is often staffed by a single physician, showing how far behind the city is in supporting EMS.
chapters.title: Narcisse thanks Ranieri and agrees EMS needs real investment

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I have a staff listening, so we can't approach it.

utterances.text: My apology that I have to be in two places at once.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I wish I could clone myself, but I'm so appreciative of it.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because someone trained for...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse

utterances.text: The police officer have their job, so they can have the CPR to keep you alive until you get the appropriate paramedic to come to take care of the person.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So thank you for sharing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And you've been here, you've been hearing that we are on your side.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We're trying to make sure we reach, because if...

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The staff not feeling good, not seeing the support, not respect, not getting the pay as well, they're not going to be able to give to deliver the care that they need to deliver.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I'm in agreement with you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: It's the position of the council that a real investment needs to be made in EMS at all levels, at the frontline provider levels, but also at the support levels.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: You know, that includes physician oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Online medical control is often staffed by a single physician.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: That's, right, if you get four or five cardiac arrests that are occurring, right, we respond, we heard today, we respond to over 80 of them a day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: If you get two or three of those at a time, that's a single physician providing clinical oversight to two or three calls at a time, in addition to some of the other calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: Again, these complex patients.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: So that's just a microcosm of...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: The how far

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Joseph Ranieri
utterances.text: behind we are in supporting an EMS as a system.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I appreciate you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we have been joined by our colleague, Guterres Jen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Paramedic Christian Bear Lopez says he testified in March and returned because problems remain, citing FDNY EMS Lieutenant Nelson Cito who died after a six-minute ambulance arrival but no one answered. He says EMS needs sustainable wages, career development, and educational pathways, and asks why the council has not assessed an independent EMS department.
chapters.title: Lopez says EMS must be a lifelong career, not a stepping stone

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Well, members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I'm Christian Bear Lopez, 25.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I'm a paramedic who's worked in EMS since graduating from St.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Francis Prep in 2019.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I testified here in March.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: FDNY EMS Lieutenant Nelson Cito served this city for over a decade.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
