utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: An ambulance arrived in six minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Nobody answered, and he left.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: His family found him dead hours later.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: His ambulance was not delayed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: It was outside his home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: The responding EMTs had less than two years on the job combined.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I started at 18, and I'm not blaming them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I'm asking why we can't retain experienced providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: We ask FDNY EMTs to spend four years in EMS to qualify for a firefighter promotion, then start over on another pay scale for another 5.5 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: We're losing experienced providers because we haven't made EMS a career worth staying in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: EMS needs sustainable wages, career development, and educational pathways into healthcare through New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: health and hospitals, but EMS itself must remain a viable, lifelong career, not merely a stepping stone into firefighting or other healthcare professions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I appreciate Councilmember Areola's transparency and her efforts towards it, but a sex notification cannot perform CPR, train an EMT, or staff an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Municipal EMS should be staffed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: To meet demand independently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Hospital ambulances and CFR fire engines should complement our EMS system, not what keeps it running.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Intro 0521 proposed an independent EMS department in 2024.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Sanitation, police, and fire have their own commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Why shouldn't EMS?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: An independent department would give EMS dedicated leadership, budget oversight, and direct accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: My generation is inheriting these problems while caring for your constituents and showing up here on our days off.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: We were essential in 2020 during the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: We're essential today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: If this council is committed to EMS reform,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Why aren't we holding a hearing and conducting a fiscal assessment on implementing Intro 0521?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Christian Bear Lopez
utterances.text: I yield my time.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Gerardney Williams, an Army veteran and paramedic, describes starting in East 86th Street and responding to East Houston Street and 121st Street with 25-minute ETAs. He says fire, police, and MTA workers all wait for ambulances, and hospitals are pulling ambulances out of the 911 system because they are not profitable.
chapters.title: Williams describes 25-minute cross-borough response times

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: How you doing?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: My name is Gerardney Williams.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I'm a United States Army veteran, former New York City correction officer, and a current New York City paramedic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I just want to start by giving a rundown on how severe response times are because of lack of staffing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So I work on an ambulance on East 86th Street and Lexington Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: And when I log on, my first caller tonight is on East Houston Street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So to go from East 86 to East Houston Street is a 25-minute ETA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: 25 minutes for an unconscious patient on the bus.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So now the bus driver has to pull over, get rid of everybody on the bus, and wait for an ambulance to get there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We get there, the patient's seizing, we stop it, we get them to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: After we clear the hospital, we get another call, 121st and 1st for domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: From East Houston to 121st and 1st, another 25-minute ETA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: The police department is there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: They can't clear the scene until the ambulance gets there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So now the MTA workers waiting for us, the police officers waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We assess that patient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: She refuses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We get to the next call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: The next call.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Old lady fell down, hit her head.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: The fire engine gets there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: fire engines waiting for us to clear the patient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So all of these response times are, they all work together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: So a fire is waiting for us, PD is waiting for us, MTA is waiting for us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: If you ever had to exit a train because you have a sick passenger, they're waiting for an ambulance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: All of this makes the city less efficient.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We have 6,000, at least 6,000 calls a day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: That's the equivalent of what we had on 9-11, what we experienced during COVID.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We're receiving those calls every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: We're in dire need of more ambulances on the street.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: In the meantime, along with the staffing issues going on with FDNY EMS, you have hospitals who contribute to the 911 system who are pulling ambulances out of the system because it's not profitable for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Hospitals are pulling ambulances out of their EMS system because it's not profitable for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I happen to work for one who pulled three ambulances out last year, got rid of the staff, laid them off, lost three ambulances from the Upper West Side, very busy area.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: This is the biggest city in the world, and we're asking for mutual aid for ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: This is shameful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: This is extremely shameful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: While I appreciate the help, the mutual aid, I think that's so...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: One, I think it's union busting also, but that's another topic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: But for us to ask for mutual aid, it's shameful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: The chief earlier mentioned the closure of hospital units, and I think it's a very important piece of this EMS thing we do here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Like he said, we do one-third of the calls in the city, but with the staff decreasing, we're doing more and more and more and more and responding to more calls out of our area, which is increasing response times.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: My ambulance sits on the Upper East Side.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: I'm responding to calls in East Harlem, Washington Heights.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Soho, Chinatown, the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: The response times are ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Today you heard two separate stories of two children being delayed care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Children in our city being delayed care because there are no EMS, there are no ambulances, there are no paramedics, there are no EMTs to respond to these calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: And I think it's just extremely important that we address the issues, FDNY pay issues, but also hospitals pulling ambulances out of the system, which is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Gerardney Williams
utterances.text: Hospitals, billion-dollar hospitals who have money to build new buildings in these neighborhoods, but somehow don't have the money to continue EMS services.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I think we spoke a little bit about that, the hospital closure and all this pulling ambulance is not right to the, yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We hear you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Andrew Freena, a former EMT and current PA, says the FDNY chief says life-threatening jobs are not held, but paramedics across all boroughs arrive under 10 minutes only 26% of the time. He says pay parity would cost a small fraction of the city budget and asks why the issue remains unsolved.
chapters.title: Freena challenges officials on political inaction over EMS pay

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: My name is Andrew Freena.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: I'm a former EMT, current PA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Not to beat a dead horse about the response times, you've heard a lot of harrowing metrics, but the FDNY commissioner, or not the commissioner, the chief, I think he said something correct that they don't hold life-threatening jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: But if you look at the statistics,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: The percentage of time across all five boroughs where the paramedics arrive under 10 minutes is 26% as of the last month, which is pretty awful.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: So you must be holding jobs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Regardless, it's nice to hear this discussion here, how everyone's recognizing that the pay is the problem and that it needs to be solved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: But it just it confuses me why the issue is not solved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: I see it as relatively simple, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: This really isn't a partisan issue, a political issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Whether you're a Democrat or Republican, a socialist, whatever, if we live in the city and our families live here, we want the ambulance to show up fast.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: I think it's what, like two, three, maybe $400 million to achieve parity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Yes, that's a lot of money, but out of $112 billion budget, it's not that much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: When you see that other agencies receive federal funds or state funds, that's another alternative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: So

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: plus the insurance billing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: There's a lot of solutions here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: And it makes me start to wonder, you know, I don't mean to say this offensively, but like, do you have your own private ambulance services or do you not live in the city?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Because aren't you worried about yourselves?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Like, I just feel like that's, you know, this is also an issue that you can be a little selfish about.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: But it frustrates me as someone who's not a politician, not a union leader.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Like, what do I do?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: I call my office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: I live in Long Island City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Thankfully, I wasn't on the ground, you know, with a compound fracture, but they don't care.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Julie Wan doesn't care, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: We call these politicians and they don't want to do much.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: And there's a lot of trying to blame the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: And then they try to blame you guys.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: And people just keep pointing the finger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: So it becomes very frustrating as a constituent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: And I just hope we can actually, you know, we're talking about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: But I hope we come to a solution now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Andrew Freena
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Walter Adler, a hospital-based paramedic and president of the EMS Public Advocacy Council, says it is painful to watch FDNY EMS bleed members. He says hospital-based EMS is not a competing force and that the different pay systems are by design.
chapters.title: Adler says hospital-based EMS stands with FDNY EMS

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: My name is Walter Adler.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I am a hospital-based paramedic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I am the president of the Emergency Medical Services Public Advocacy Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I'm also an 1199 delegate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I'm here today as a paramedic who works for the voluntary hospitals to say it is painful and shameful to watch what is happening to the bleeding of FDNY EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We see how their union leaders are struggling, organizing, negotiating, fighting for 4.6 years is what it now feels like.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And we give them respect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We see their members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We do our jobs with their members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I'm the ALS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I have some Fidney BLS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I began my career as a scared little 18-year-old working for TransCare in Canarsie.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I became a Midwood Teamster.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I was in 2507 for four years as a fire department EMT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And now I'm a proud, proud, proud member of 1199 at a hospital.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And I will say this, above all else, I am a paramedic and I was an EMT.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And I want our brothers and sisters in Fidney to know that we're not a competing force.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We're out here with them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We get paid completely different ways in different sectors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: But that is by design.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: It is not that there's like a villain in this story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: The council makes resolutions that say parity is important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Mayors make promises.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: They do their best.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: The OLR isn't a hateful group of people, so we think.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Everybody's trying their best to get justice for our municipal EMS workforce.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And we, the about 3,000 members of the 1199 hospital-based EMS, with our brothers and sisters in Presbyterian, who are non-union, we are saying we are not a competing force and we see you out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: That then said...

chapters.summary: Adler says the city must reduce call volume by 10%, reclaim EMS members who went to fire, and reduce CFR use when not necessary. He also calls for ending the fire promotional pathway, public education on 911 overuse, and a serious conversation about an independent EMS department.
chapters.title: Adler lists solutions: reduce call volume, end fire promotion, EMS department

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: I think there have been solutions introduced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: The most important ones I would just like to list off in whatever time I have remaining because they are important and they are not being considered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Everyone says, where is this $200 to $400 million to pay Finney EMS going to come from?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And the answer is we need to reduce call volume in this city by 10%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: That is in the citizen budget report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We need to use medic and EMT units.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We need to use firefighter and EMT units, and we need to reclaim the EMS that have gone to fire to be a resource,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: and we need to reduce CFR utilization except when necessary because it is more expensive to send five people that make $109K than send two people that make $57K.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: This is all the 2018 Citizen Budget Commission, and I believe it should inform us where some of the money could come from and things that could be acceptable to the UFA and 2507.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Finally, I know I'm over time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: There is something called the Gilbay Malay proposal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: They are senior members.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: They are paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Their first thing is well known to everybody.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: We want to get Fidney EMS to 109K after five years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: of service or as close to, that is our conception of parity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Two, we need to end the promotional to fire because people should not use our field as a stepping stone and it closes the gap and attracts people from other sectors that want to make a career.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Third thing, we need to educate the public on 911 overuse, abuse, and misuse because if the public is truly educated about what is 911 calls, we go from 6,000 calls to 3,000 and then it can be handled by the various

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: alignments we have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Finally,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Brannan introduced the independent department of EMS on behalf and in solidarity with Local 2507 and 3621, not because anybody wants to wrench EMS out of the hands of the fire department,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: but a serious conversation has to be had about 70 actors that are deploying ambulances, four sectors, 10 unions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And if we do not force that conversation through a department of EMS that does not necessarily need to command and control all ambulances, then we are

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: creating piecemeal solutions, which respectfully, Chair Areola, I understand what your local laws do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: They create accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: They create structure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: But our men and women are dying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Our citizens are dying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: And it feels often like the city and OLR and the mayor is dancing in a circle around us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Walter Adler
utterances.text: Sorry to go over.

chapters.summary: Jack Chapman of 1199 says EMS starting salaries around $40,000 are not competitive in New York City and lag behind firefighters, driving attrition. He says ALS call volumes have increased while hospitals remove voluntary ambulances, and ALS units are often sent to calls BLS units could handle.
chapters.title: Chapman says EMS pay is not competitive and ALS units are misused

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Good afternoon, members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: I'd like to first thank the committees for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: It is imperative that we discuss the importance of maintaining efficient ambulance response times in a city that houses over 8 million people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: My name is Jack Chapman, and I am here on behalf of 1199 and the EMS workers that we represent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: I've been working in EMS for over 15 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: I think I can skip reading the statistics on the increasing response times at this point, as it has been well discussed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: There are many reasons for the rising delays in response times across New York City, including staffing shortages, higher call volumes, low pay, packed emergency departments, and hospitals removing their voluntary ambulances from the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Much like other parts of our healthcare system, EMS has been affected by exacerbating staffing shortages and funding being taken out of healthcare.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: EMS personnel across FDNY and private ambulances have an average starting salaries around $40,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: In a city as large and expensive as this, and for a job that can be both physically and mentally taxing, these wages are not competitive or attractive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: One could make the same amount of money simply taking advantage of the newly required hourly pay for delivery app drivers, and there would be no intensive training or prerequisites.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: EMS personnel wages also lag behind firefighters, with many who are already in the FDNY system eventually leaving to become firefighters themselves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Approximately 4,300 EMTs and paramedics left their positions between fiscal year 2019 and 2020.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: In addition to increasing staffing shortages we are seeing in EMS, ALS call volumes across the city have increased over the past decade, outpacing non-life-threatening medical emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: And the life-threatening medical emergencies have increased by 22.9% since 2015, compared with a 2.5% increase of non-life-threatening emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: This increase is also happening at a time when many hospitals are reducing voluntary ambulance services from the 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: So EMS personnel are now being asked to take on a bigger workload with an increase of ALS calls while working with an understaffed team and being paid minimal wages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: The city's first responders play a critical role in ensuring the health and safety of those living here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: And they are here in the event of illness or injury to provide on-scene treatment and transport to a hospital, but are being tasked with providing those services without the resources necessary to do so efficiently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: While FDNY recognizes the shortage of paramedics that they have, they do not have an active pathway to recruit credentialed paramedics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Certified paramedics must join as EMTs and then be accepted to the department's paramedic program to then go through almost a year of paramedic school again when they're already credentialed to do this job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: It's also worth noting that many calls are often triaged in ways that upgrade them to require an ALS-level response, just for the ALS providers to arrive on scene to find a patient that does not require the interventions that they are able to provide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: ALS units are regularly sent to calls that BLS units are more than capable of.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: capable of handling, which results in less ALS units being available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: The system is understaffed and overworked.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: We are now at a point that we are seeing NYPD seek out alternative resources when they are unable to get an ambulance on scene because the EMS system is in such backlog.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: There are many factors that have led us to where we are now, which is resulting in ambulances not being able to arrive in a timely manner to those who truly need them the most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: The time is now to effect meaningful change and provide our members with the pay and resources they need to effectively continue to provide rapid, on-scene care and transport for those who need it most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: One of our union officers just told me about an event that just happened at the nearby Virgin Hotel this past Saturday.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Where it took 40 minutes for EMS to respond to a stat ep, which is short for status epilepticus, and simply put stands for ongoing or prolonged seizures, and is a true life-threatening emergency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Over 40 minutes for EMS to get on scene.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Chronic abusers of the 911 system, many of whom call daily, call themselves in in a way that identifies them as high-priority emergencies and take that resource away from those who need them the most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Recognizing that that does not mean these individuals do not deserve a response, the city should try to find a way to identify this and create a plan to minimize wasting the resources that are so wasted every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

chapters.summary: Stephen Northmore, a FDNY EMS rescue medic, recounts a cardiac patient waiting 40 minutes for an ambulance, a patient with three broken limbs waiting 50 minutes, and a child waiting 30 minutes while a fire company was on scene. He says these cases show the system is out of time.
chapters.title: Northmore recounts delayed responses for critical patients

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: My name is Stephen Northmore and I am representing myself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: I have been a member of FDNY EMS for the past 14 years, starting in 2012 as an EMT, then paramedic, hashtag medic, and finally rescue medic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: We are out of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: I have firsthand account in the last month that a patient waited 40 minutes for an ambulance to be assigned after they had started showing symptoms of a life-threatening cardiac condition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: A crew confided in me the next day that the same previous day as the cardiac patient, a patient who had suffered a serious accident with three of their limbs broken, which if not handled correctly could cause a fatal bleed or nerve damage causing permanent disability, had waited

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: 50 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: For an ambulance to arrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: A few weeks ago in Brooklyn, I heard a fire company over the radio that had been waiting at the scene of an injured child for 30 minutes, who can compensate and appear very well after injury until they suddenly rapidly deteriorate, be told that there were no ambulances available.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Another crew a few weeks ago confided in me that their patient had died from a manageable bleed while waiting 40 minutes for an ambulance to be dispatched.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: I'd heard of another pediatric patient with an obviously and painfully broken arm, again, if not handled correctly, could lead to a life-threatening bleed or permanent disability, had waited an hour for an ambulance to arrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: That same crew informed me another patient of theirs with an immobilizing broken bone had waited three hours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: hours for an ambulance a couple of weeks before.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: A toddler with a critical second-degree burn from boiling liquid spilt on them waiting in their mother's arms for 30 minutes for an ambulance to be dispatched.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: This is the testimony of one member out of thousands.

chapters.summary: Northmore says the city's line of credit from EMS workers has run out and the situation was willed into existence by officials who ignored warnings. He says every other fix has been tried except fair pay, which is the wound bleeding EMS of personnel, morale, and experience.
chapters.title: Northmore says the city has run out of credit and must stop the bleeding

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: The line of credit this city's and state's legislatures and executives have taken out for decades from the rare and exceptional people willing to descend into these situations for shameful compensation and disrespect has run out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: This situation has not been brought on by some force of nature or act of God.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: It has been willed into existence by past city council members being informed of a clear and present danger to the citizens of this city and stating, moving on to new business.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: It hasn't been manifested by a weather emergency or pandemic, but by past mayors stating the work is different to justify our racist and sexist second-class first responder status for decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: True, the member of this council's mayor of the city and government of this state have not overseen the decades of belittling and undervaluing of the members who take care of people hit by trains,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: seizing on sidewalks, lost all of their skin in fires, drowning in their own fluids from pregnancy complications, entangled, maimed in heavy machinery, or descending into the darkness of pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: I do commend the members of this committee who have spoken out and are proposing these measures, but as any member of this city's emergency system,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Services will tell you the people of this city do not want to hear words of comfort with our arrival.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: They demand action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: The commissioners have sounded the alarms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: The chief have sounded alarms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: The unions have sounded the alarms.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: The EMS service has followed every avenue to prevent this, and they have failed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Hospital liaison units, paramedic response units, tactical response groups, mutual aid ambulances, closest hospital transports, volunteer ambulances, one-for-one relief mandated over times,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: all to ignore the bleeding, seizing, wheezing, inconvenient truth in the corner of the room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: I've seen every other measure to fix this system tried and failed except the primary one that almost every member agrees on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Our pay that is as fair as the separate but equal policies of this nation's past.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: It will not fix all the problems with this system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: But unless this pay issue is addressed, I have no confidence any other measure will exceed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Succeed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: It is the wound that is bleeding us of personnel, morale, resources, wisdom, experience, and talent, from the ranks of EMT to paramedic to lieutenant to captain to chiefs to even our supervising doctors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: The past remedy has been only to pump in new blood as we bleed out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: You do not have to be a doctor, medic, or EMT to know when faced with what to address first, pumping in new blood or stopping the bleeding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Stop the bleeding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: The EMTs, paramedics, and officers and doctors of FDNY EMS will continue to answer the rising tide of emergency calls in this city on

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: under solemn oath and dwindling resources, with the blood on our boots, placenta fluid on our pants, and cerebral spinal fluid on our sleeves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: We await for the appropriate response to this clear and present danger to the citizens and visitors of the city of New York from all the other oath-takers for the public safety and public good.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Thank you, and may God bless the members of EMS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: James Carr, former executive director of NYC EMS, says response time is a symptom of broader problems the fire department cannot solve alone. He recommends a mayor-directed EMS improvement and modernization task force bringing together FDNY, OMB, OLR, labor, H&H, and hospitals to produce an implementation plan within 90 days.
chapters.title: Carr proposes mayor-directed EMS improvement task force

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: My name is James Carr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: I served as executive director of New York City EMS from 1980 to 1988.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: And this man's testimony was the best introduction I could possibly have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: I want to tell you that although there have been, I think, some changes in EMS in almost 40 years since I left,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Sadly, many of those challenges still remain today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: And I have to say that we talked about problems with response time, and response time is clearly a symptom, not an isolated issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: It's a symptom of other problems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The thing is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The mayor has to take responsibility for this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Happily, I no longer work for any mayors or anyone in the city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: And I want to tell you that the things that have been talked about today, from the beginning of this meeting until today, until right now,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: are things that some of which the fire department has control over, but many of those things the fire department does not have control over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: They need help, as this gentleman went through in a quite articulate manner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The fire department can't address these challenges by itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: I'm recommending a mayor-directed EMS improvement and modernization task force, bringing together the fire department, OMB,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: OLR, EMS labor, health and hospitals in the broader hospital community to put together, to work together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: To focus not on finger-pointing, but to work together as a team to try to figure out the various issues and responses to the various issues that are necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: It's very clear.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: You don't have to be a rocket scientist to recognize that they need competitive pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: They need, dare I say, parity with the fire department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: In addition to that, if you want to deal with the increased call volume, you're going to need more staff than you currently have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: I'm talking about staff beyond the 45,000 that they currently have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Yes, they're at 41,000 or whatever the number was, 4,150 or whatever.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: But the goal is 45.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: But the goal is 45.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: But there's been a 41% increase since the 20-teens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Did their budget increase, their budget for staff, increase by 41%?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: I'll tell you the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: So the mayor has to put this, has to be the convening person who puts this group together, people who work for him, who have to collaborate with one another to address these issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: And I'm proposing that within 90 days, the task force submit an implementation plan that establishes clinically appropriate response time targets, identifies the staff,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: ambulance capacity, and operational improvements needed to meet those targets, and specifying the resources required and the agencies responsible for implementation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The process could be measured by the percentage of patients reached within those targets.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: And what I'm saying is you want an ALS unit 95% of the time in six minutes, not an average.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Of 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Because the averages cover up an awful lot of outlier calls.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The outlier calls are the things that we're talking about here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The difficulty is that it's not one or two outliers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: It's tons of outliers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The system-wide problem requires a system-wide management response, and New York City, I believe, has the data, the expertise, and the technology to improve EMS performance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: What is needed is a coordinated mechanism to turn that knowledge into action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: The objective is faster, more reliable access to appropriate care and better patient outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - James Carr
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola thanks the in-person public panel and says there has never been such focus on EMS failure. Narcisse tells Stephen Northmore that the chair is a fighter and that the committees will follow up, not just listen.
chapters.title: Ariola and Narcisse close in-person testimony and pledge follow-up

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Any questions for this?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I just want to let, what's the name again?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: Stephen North.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Stephen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I just want you to know that Chair worked very hard, and she's a fighter.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's not that we're sitting here just to listen.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And she's surely going to follow.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We're all going to follow up.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I'm in to support what's going on as a registrar.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So we hear you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: We're not here just to talk.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: I recognize that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephen Northmore
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And I said it before, and I'll say it again.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: I don't think there's ever been a time when there's been such focus on the fact that EMS has failed.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: In the way it is now.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And this mayor inherited this problem, but he is the mayor now, and it's his job to solve it.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: And we'll be there to assist him in doing that.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So thank you.

chapters.summary: Ariola concludes the in-person Q&A panel and transitions to virtual panelists. She explains that staff will unmute each witness when their name is called and the sergeant at arms will set the timer.
chapters.title: Ariola opens virtual testimony and explains unmuting process

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: That's the end of our in-person Q&A panel.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: So it has been concluded.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: We will now turn to virtual panelists.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: For virtual panelists, once your name is called, a member of our staff will unmute you, and the Sergeant at Arms will set the timer and give you the go-ahead to begin.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Please wait for the sergeant to announce that you may begin before delivering your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Now I will call our first virtual panelist, Tyler Weaver.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Tyler Weaver says his 24-year-old son Nikos Costello suffered cardiac arrest in the Bronx in 2023 and waited 20 minutes for an ambulance, leading to severe brain damage and death. He says cardiac arrest revival rates have dropped from 20% to 16% and response times have returned to early 1980s levels.
chapters.title: Tyler Weaver testifies about son Nikos and falling survival rates

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: My name is Tyler Weaver.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: I wish to thank the council and chairpersons Areola and Narcisse for hosting this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: As I said to this committee two years ago, you know, my 24 year old son, Nikos Costello, suffered a cardiac arrest in the Bronx in 2023.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Unfortunately, it took an ambulance 20 minutes to reach him, and due to severe brain damage from too many minutes without enough oxygen, he was declared dead in ICU the next day and taken off life support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: And the loss of Nick, of course, has been a heavy blow to my family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Four years ago, the MMR reported a cardiac arrest revival rate of 20%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Two years ago that dropped to 17% and then last year dropped down to 16%.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: With the 20,000 or so cardiac arrests each year, that's a one-fifth relative drop in revival is significant and it means hundreds of less New Yorkers were revived.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Back in June 1981, the average response time to critical calls by EMS was 13 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: And we just heard from Jim Carr, who was there at that time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: And under his leadership, they were able to lower that down, I think, all the way down to nine minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: So there's ways to solve this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Even during 2020, when COVID hit,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: The final average for that year was 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: However, since 2017, response time to life-threatening calls has been increasing, and for the first time in 40 years, it just hit 13 minutes again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: So this milestone should be a major wake-up call to everyone that the city has now gone back to ambulance response times from the early 1980s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Incredibly, the situation continues to get even worse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Monthly averages recently reached 15 minutes and the Bronx even hit 18 minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: FDNY EMS workers get paid a lot less than other first responders, so it's no wonder why they keep leaving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: They haven't had a contract in four years and the downstream effect is that they're understaffed by 400 positions and numerous up to 100 ambulances are left sitting unstaffed daily.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: I believe that increasing EMS pay, renewing their contract will be one important part of fixing the response time crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: And the mayor and the officer labor relations should re-examine their priorities and their overall approach to EMS labor issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: In the meantime, all major EMS stats keep going in the wrong direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: And New Yorkers in medical distress are suffering harm while waiting too long for ambulances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: And I want to thank you for having me here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tyler Weaver
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Weaver, we just want you to know that we will not give up until EMS.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: brings their response times down, and a tragedy that you have suffered will never happen again to any other family.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Thank you so much for always showing up for the hearings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jack Chapman
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Next, we have Cheryl Bernard.

chapters.summary: Retired NYPD communications member Cheryl Bernard says increasing population, hospital closures, and retirements all affect response times, but DOT's bus lanes, bike lanes, and street thinning are a major problem. She describes an ambulance unable to pass due to a protected bike lane and warns against giving the public ETAs.
chapters.title: Cheryl Bernard blames DOT street redesigns for ambulance delays

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: Hi, can you all hear me?

utterances.speaker: Joann Ariola
utterances.text: Yes, we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: Hi, how are you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: Good evening, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: My name is Cheryl Bernard, and I want to say afternoon to the chair members, the city council, the members of the Committee on Fire and Emergency Management Hospitals, and everyone involved in this meeting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: I want to say thank you to EMS and their FD for their service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: I myself, I'm a retired member, 29 years of NYPD for communication division that oversees 911 system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: So trust me, I know about the calls that come in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: I also want to say my condolences to the family of Nick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: My comment is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: Population and housing increasing, hospitals decreasing, NYPD, FDNY, and EMS workers retiring, all these situations make response times decrease.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: I am all for the pay increase.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: I am definitely for that because as one on the receiving end, we definitely need more money and we're underpaid.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: But you can increase the pay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: You can remove personnel from the deck.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: desktop, you can put them in a field, everything else you can think of, the common denominator here and the main problem is DOT's active project of bus lanes, bike lanes, and street thinning and street closures and rerouting.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: I have a video where ambulance was called to an emergency on Rutland and Kingston.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: No traffic can pass because the newly installed protected bike lane

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: No one can pass.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: In the video, there's no bikes traveling on a bike lane, but all the cars were backed up and they had to find another route to leave.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: Can you imagine if this was reversed?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: Let's say that, and this happens, we're in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard
utterances.text: So someone had an emergency that's a car driver who required medical attention and the ambulance was behind the traffic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Cheryl Bernard

chapters.summary: FDNY EMT Christopher McKagan, a 27-year veteran, takes issue with the statement that EMS has failed and says the city government has failed EMS. summary: The Committee on Fire and Emergency Management, jointly with the Committee on Hospitals, held an oversight hearing on ambulance response times and Intro 990, which would require Notify NYC alerts for extended ambulance dispatch delays.

FDNY leaders acknowledged rising response times, declining ambulance hours, staffing losses, hospital closures, and recruitment challenges, while raising concerns about Intro 990's notification volume.

Council members, EMS unions, current and former EMS workers, IBO analysts, and public witnesses described pay disparities, attrition, delayed responses, and preventable deaths, urging pay parity, retention investments, and accountability.
title: Committee on Fire and Emergency Management
